prompt: Write a tragic love story about a lord's daughter falling in love with a servant.

outline.name: The House on the Hill
outline.description: Introduce rain-soaked Valedorn, Greyfen Manor, and the declining House Vey. Lady Elianor observes the estate’s debts, hungry tenants, overworked servants, and her father Lord Alric’s desperate attempts to preserve their lineage. Though treated as a privileged daughter, she feels trapped by the obligations attached to her birth. Alric announces that her marriage to the wealthy Lord Caelan Arbridge is the family’s only hope, establishing the central conflict between duty, compassion, and personal freedom.

outline.name: A Favorable Match
outline.description: Elianor meets Lord Caelan formally at Greyfen. He is polished, intelligent, and courteous in a way that reveals his sense of ownership rather than affection. During negotiations, Caelan makes clear that marriage will give him control over Greyfen’s debts, land, and household. Elianor privately challenges her father about the arrangement, but Alric argues that refusing would ruin the estate and deprive every servant and tenant of protection. Elianor accepts the betrothal, concealing her dread beneath perfect composure.

outline.name: The Falconer’s Son
outline.description: Elianor begins escaping the manor’s suffocating routines by walking in the neglected woods. There she encounters Tomas Vale, the head falconer’s son, who reacts warily to her presence while tending an injured goshawk in an abandoned forester’s lodge. Their conversation is tense: Elianor offers medicine from the manor, while Tomas refuses to flatter her and points out the suffering her family’s authority has caused. Despite their differences, she returns the next day with linen and food, beginning an uneasy connection.

outline.name: Willow Splints
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas work together to treat the goshawk’s broken wing. Their practical cooperation allows them to speak more freely. Tomas explains the risks faced by servants and tenants, including his mother’s death after eviction from a Vey cottage. Elianor admits that privilege has left her isolated and unable to choose her own life. Tomas remains suspicious of her motives, but her willingness to listen begins to change his opinion. Their secret meetings become a recurring refuge.

outline.name: The Shape of Rain
outline.description: As the goshawk slowly recovers, Elianor and Tomas grow closer through stolen hours in the woods. They share food, a cloak, memories, and small confessions. Elianor sees Tomas’s pride and tenderness beneath his guarded manner, while Tomas recognizes that her compassion is more than aristocratic sentiment. Their attraction becomes impossible to deny, though both understand the danger. A near-discovery by a passing groom forces them to separate abruptly and reminds them that their refuge is not safe.

outline.name: The First Flight
outline.description: The goshawk attempts its first flight after its recovery, symbolizing the possibility of freedom that neither lover can yet claim. Tomas and Elianor celebrate beneath the trees, and their restraint finally breaks into a kiss. They acknowledge that their love is forbidden and cannot be made respectable by secrecy. Elianor returns to Greyfen changed, struggling to perform her duties while carrying the memory of the kiss. Tomas warns her that discovery could cost him his life, but neither can bring themselves to end the meetings.

outline.name: Ledgers and Debts
outline.description: The financial crisis at Greyfen worsens. Alric reviews debt ledgers with Elianor and reveals that Caelan can call in the family’s obligations unless the marriage proceeds quickly. Elianor discovers that several tenants are being forced into unpaid labor to compensate for the estate’s losses. She attempts to persuade her father to reduce rents, but he insists that weakness will invite seizure by stronger lords. Caelan arrives to supervise the negotiations, observing Elianor and Tomas from a distance and beginning to suspect their relationship.

outline.name: A Courtesy of Chains
outline.description: Caelan begins exerting control without openly breaking etiquette. He recommends changes to Greyfen’s accounts, dismisses a groom, and offers to take responsibility for managing the estate after the wedding. In private, he questions Elianor about her absences and subtly reminds her that her father’s survival depends on obedience. Tomas notices Caelan watching him and becomes more guarded. Caelan threatens Tomas’s father through an accusation of theft, making clear that the entire household can be punished for one servant’s presumed insolence.

outline.name: The Housekeeper’s Message
outline.description: Tomas meets Mara Quill, a former Greyfen housekeeper who now carries messages among tenant and laborer resistance groups. She explains that nobles across Valedorn are using debt, forced labor, and manipulated courts to seize land. Tomas is tempted by the movement’s promise of dignity, though he fears that rebellion will endanger Elianor. Mara argues that private love cannot survive a public system built on ownership. Tomas agrees to carry a message, beginning his involvement while keeping it secret from Elianor.

outline.name: The Cost of Silence
outline.description: Elianor learns that a village family has been expelled from its cottage after failing to meet a labor demand. She confronts Alric and discovers that he approved the eviction to satisfy Caelan’s creditors. Her father insists that every harsh decision is meant to preserve Greyfen and protect its people from a worse fate. Elianor sees how fear has made him complicit. When she meets Tomas, he challenges her to decide whether sympathy without action is simply another form of silence. Their disagreement briefly wounds their intimacy.

outline.name: The Rebel Road
outline.description: Tomas travels with Mara through the marsh villages and witnesses the breadth of noble exploitation. He meets discharged soldiers, tenant leaders, and laborers preparing to resist. The rebels plan to seize or destroy ledgers proving illegal debts and land seizures. Tomas returns to Greyfen torn between the movement’s purpose and his attachment to Elianor. He tells her only that unrest is spreading, and she realizes he is keeping a dangerous part of his life from her. Their trust becomes strained by unequal risks and concealed loyalties.

outline.name: Winter Betrothal
outline.description: Lord Alric publicly announces that Elianor and Caelan will marry before spring. Preparations force Elianor into elaborate fittings, social visits, and rehearsals of obedience. Caelan privately promises that Tomas and his father may retain employment if Elianor behaves, but he implies that after the wedding the household will be reorganized under his authority. Elianor understands that her marriage may preserve Greyfen only by surrendering it. She asks Alric to guarantee the servants’ safety, and he accepts without grasping the personal cost of the request.

outline.name: The Assassin’s Question
outline.description: Mara reveals that Caelan will gather regional lords at Greyfen to finalize the transfer of Vey lands and coordinate reprisals against suspected rebels. The resistance faction demands that Tomas assassinate Caelan during the gathering. Tomas refuses to become a murderer, even though Mara argues that Caelan’s death could prevent the crushing of the rebellion. She warns that Caelan has already ordered raids and that Elianor will not be safe within his household. Tomas leaves uncertain whether restraint is moral courage or cowardice.

outline.name: A Bargain with Winter
outline.description: Elianor decides to accept the marriage in the belief that she can protect Greyfen’s dependents through compromise. She tells Tomas she will marry Caelan and asks him to understand that she is sacrificing herself for the household. Tomas is devastated, hearing only that she has chosen privilege over him. Their argument exposes the limits of both their ideals: Elianor trusts negotiation with men who have never honored it, while Tomas trusts rebellion that may demand blood. They part angrily, though their love remains unmistakable.

outline.name: The Last Hunting Season
outline.description: The manor prepares for the wedding while winter storms isolate Greyfen. Elianor attempts to use her remaining authority to improve rations and delay evictions, but Caelan counters each effort through debt claims and his influence over Alric. Tomas learns from stable hands that Caelan intends to dismiss many Vey servants after the marriage. He and Mara begin planning an escape route through the woods and marsh. Elianor finds Tomas again, and their anger gives way to a fragile reconciliation.

outline.name: Beyond the Marsh
outline.description: Tomas proposes that he and Elianor flee before the wedding, cross the marsh, and reach a rebel safehouse beyond the border. Elianor fears abandoning the servants and tenants, but Tomas argues that remaining will make them both instruments of Caelan’s power. For one night they imagine a difficult life together without titles or estates. They share a final tender night in the forester’s lodge and promise to meet there before dawn. Unknown to them, Caelan has begun pressuring members of the household for information.

outline.name: The Betrayal
outline.description: Elianor secretly leaves Greyfen in plain clothing and reaches the lodge, where Tomas is waiting with provisions and a route through the marsh. Before they can depart, soldiers surround the building. Their escape has been betrayed by a frightened servant coerced by Caelan, though the betrayer’s identity remains uncertain. Tomas tries to lead Elianor away while surrendering himself, but both are captured. The failed flight destroys their hope of remaining hidden and gives Caelan the evidence he needs to control the entire Vey household.

outline.name: A Public Shame
outline.description: Caelan stages a public hearing in Greyfen’s courtyard, presenting Tomas as a trespasser and would-be abductor while exposing Elianor’s relationship to humiliate her. Alric, terrified of losing the estate, cannot defend his daughter openly. Tomas is beaten and sentenced to hang for violating noble property and attempting to flee with a lady. Elianor is confined to her rooms until the wedding. Caelan expects scandal to make her submissive, but his cruelty convinces her that every compromise has only strengthened him.

outline.name: The Locked Room
outline.description: Confined in her rooms, Elianor reflects on the choices that brought her there and hears rumors of reprisals against villages connected to the rebels. She confronts Alric, demanding that he acknowledge what Caelan has done. He admits that he has surrendered authority piece by piece because he feared losing the family name. Elianor rejects his version of duty. Meanwhile, household women and stable hands begin quietly communicating with her, revealing that Tomas’s punishment has united servants who had previously feared acting.

outline.name: The Women of Greyfen
outline.description: The household women devise a plan to free Elianor from confinement, using wedding preparations, laundry passages, and a distracted guard detail. Elianor learns that rebel sympathizers are hidden among the workers arriving for the wedding and that Mara is trying to reach the estate. She must decide whether to escape alone or return to the courtyard where Tomas will die. Refusing another private sacrifice, she chooses open defiance. The servants help disguise her and arm her with proof of Caelan’s abuses from the estate records.

outline.name: The Gallows in the Rain
outline.description: On the morning of the execution, Elianor reaches the courtyard as Tomas is brought to the gallows. Before the gathered servants, tenants, and nobles, she denounces Caelan and reads evidence of illegal seizures, forced labor, and manipulated debts. Her speech transforms private fear into collective outrage. Caelan orders the guards to silence her, but the stable hands barricade the gates and the workers attack the execution party. The revolt begins within Greyfen itself.

outline.name: The Manor Breaks
outline.description: Chaos spreads through Greyfen as servants seize keys, tenants storm the stores, and rebels among the workers disarm guards. Tomas escapes and immediately helps others rather than pursuing Caelan. Elianor leads a group toward the armory and records room, using her knowledge of the manor’s hidden passages. Alric tries to stop the uprising, then witnesses Caelan’s men attacking unarmed household members and finally turns against the lord who has consumed his authority. The estate’s old hierarchy collapses in a single violent day.

outline.name: The Burning Ledgers
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas reach the records room and uncover ledgers documenting generations of debt, forced labor, and fraudulent land claims. They distribute copies to tenant representatives before setting the records ablaze. Caelan retreats toward the chapel with armed followers, intending to preserve the documents and seize Elianor as a hostage. Tomas insists on opening the manor gates so the servants can escape before confronting him. Elianor wants to remain at Tomas’s side, but he makes her promise to carry the evidence and the people to safety.

outline.name: Dawn at Greyfen
outline.description: Tomas confronts Caelan near the chapel. He refuses to kill him, declaring that the new world cannot be founded on the same ownership and vengeance that shaped the old one. Caelan shoots Tomas before being overwhelmed by the rebels. Mortally wounded, Tomas helps Elianor and the servants open the gates and escape the burning manor, collapsing only after the last prisoners are free. Lord Alric dies amid the destruction, unable to restore the order he sacrificed everything to preserve. At dawn, Elianor holds Tomas as he dies in the rain, with the healed goshawk circling overhead.

outline.name: What Remains
outline.description: After the revolt, Elianor inherits a ruined, bankrupt Greyfen while Caelan survives to face the wider rebellion and its uncertain justice. She refuses his claims, opens the manor stores, and protects servants and tenants from immediate retaliation. Over the following years, she sells portions of the estate, abolishes hereditary service on the remaining lands, and works with rebel leaders to create courts where tenants can challenge noble authority. She is condemned as a traitor by many nobles and remembered as a liberator by others. Elianor continues to mourn Tomas, honoring his request by turning grief into practical freedom rather than a monument to their love. Greyfen remains marked by rain and loss, but no longer depends on fear.

chapters.name: The House on the Hill
chapters.content:
Rain had made a gray kingdom of Valedorn.

It silvered the fields, filled the wheel ruts, and hung from the black branches of the ash trees. Beyond the hill, the village roofs crouched beneath the weather. Smoke from their chimneys was thin and uncertain, pressed back toward the ground.

Greyfen Manor stood above them all.

Its oldest tower had been built when the Vey family still kept hawks for kings. Ivy strangled the eastern wing, three windows were boarded against drafts, and the slate roof over the servants’ hall sagged between the chimneys. Yet from a distance Greyfen remained imposing: a house of towers and gables, a stern crown upon the hill.

Lady Elianor Vey watched it through the carriage window as she returned from the lower farms.

Her maid, Sella, sat opposite with a basket of damp linens at her feet and one hand pressed against her stomach. She had been ill since morning, though she insisted it was only the weather.

“You should have stayed at the manor,” Elianor said.

“And let you go alone among the tenants?” Sella gave a tired smile. “Then everyone would say I have grown lazy.”

“Everyone says you work too hard.”

“Everyone has never been a servant.”

The carriage jolted through a flooded rut. Sella caught the basket before it tipped. Mud splashed the window, briefly obscuring the village below.

When the view cleared, Elianor saw the cottage at the edge of the south field.

Its door was gone. A family’s belongings lay beneath a torn canvas beside the wall: a stool, a cracked basin, two blankets, and a child’s wooden horse darkened by rain. The father stood with his back to the road, trying to hold the canvas over the smaller children. Their mother had gathered the eldest against her breast.

“Stop the carriage.”

Sella’s expression tightened. “My lady—”

“Stop.”

The coachman obeyed. Elianor opened the door and crossed the verge, lifting her skirts from the mud.

The family looked up as she approached. Fear moved through them faster than recognition.

The man bowed awkwardly. “My lady.”

“Why are you outside?”

His wife pulled the children closer.

The man glanced toward the road, where the estate bailiff’s cart had vanished. “We could not meet the labor demand.”

“What labor demand?”

“The one written in the notice.”

Elianor knew the notices. They had multiplied over the past year, nailed to doors and gateposts in the same careful hand: additional ditching, hauling, and days owed in lieu of rent. She had seen them stacked beside her father’s letters, but had never asked how many days a body could give before it became nothing but labor.

“The harvest failed,” the man said. “The river took the lower barley. We asked for time.”

“And the bailiff refused?”

“He said Lord Vey’s debts could not wait for the weather.”

Rain ran from Elianor’s hood into her eyes. She looked at the children, the wooden horse, the bare threshold behind them.

“I will speak to my father,” she said.

The man lowered his head. “That is kind of you, my lady.”

It was not kindness. It was the only thing she knew to offer, and suddenly it seemed small enough to shame her.

Back at Greyfen, servants carried coal from the kitchen stores to the upper rooms. The fire in the entrance hall had gone out, though the hearth was piled with ash. Elianor passed two footmen wringing water from their sleeves and found Sella waiting beneath the gallery.

“You must change,” Sella said. “You are dripping on the floor.”

“Did you see the family at the south cottage?”

“I saw the carriage stop.”

“Why did no one tell me they were being turned out?”

Sella glanced toward the portrait of Lord Edric Vey, whose painted eyes seemed to judge everyone beneath him. “Perhaps no one wanted to be the one to tell you.”

“Why?”

“Because you are Lady Elianor.”

The answer followed her upstairs.

Her rooms were warm, though the fire had been fed with furniture from the disused west wing. A carved chair burned in the grate, one of a matching set that had belonged to her grandmother. Elianor stood before it until a brass ornament blackened and fell into the coals.

On her desk lay three unopened letters and a copy of the household accounts. She had begun reading them in secret three months earlier, first because the sums frightened her, and then because ignorance frightened her more.

The Vey debts filled six ledgers.

There were loans against the east pasture, the mill, the timber rights, and the manor’s silver. Interest had been borrowed to pay interest. Repairs had been postponed until the roof itself became a debt. The family owed merchants in Harrowmere, lenders in the capital, and two neighboring lords who had once called Lord Alric their friend.

At the bottom of the latest account, in her father’s cramped hand, was a single line:

If Arbridge calls the notes, Greyfen is lost.

She touched the words.

A knock came at the door.

“Enter.”

Sella stepped in carrying a dry gown. Behind her came Master Hobb, the old steward, his shoulders bent beneath a rain-dark cloak.

“His lordship requests you in the library,” Hobb said.

“Is he ill?”

“Not in the manner physicians can mend.”

The library smelled of damp leather and extinguished candles. Lord Alric stood beside the tall windows, though the view offered only rain and blurred elms. He had grown thinner in the past year. His dark hair, once touched with silver, was now almost entirely gray, and his right hand trembled when he held a glass.

He did not turn as Elianor entered.

“You went to the south farms.”

“Yes.”

“I asked you not to concern yourself with estate matters.”

“You asked me to concern myself with the estate. Those are not the same thing.”

His shoulders stiffened. “You have been speaking with Hobb.”

“I can read.”

“That has always been your difficulty.”

She removed her wet gloves. “A family has been evicted from the south cottage.”

“Their rent is six months in arrears.”

“Their harvest failed.”

“The harvest failed for everyone.”

“Then why are only the poor punished for it?”

Alric turned. Weariness had hollowed his face.

“You think I do not know what is happening?”

“I think you know and continue to permit it.”

“The cottage belongs to Greyfen. The labor owed to Greyfen is written into the tenancy. If I forgive every debt because the weather is cruel, the estate will not survive another winter.”

“Perhaps the estate should not survive.”

For a moment, he looked not like a lord but an old man wounded by his own child.

“And what would you preserve instead?” he asked. “The walls? The family name? Or the people who depend upon both?”

“The people depend upon food, Father. Not on the name Vey.”

“You are young.”

“I am not blind.”

“No.” He went to the desk and opened the nearest ledger. “You see one family in the rain. I see three hundred families who will be without seed if Greyfen’s creditors seize the grain stores. I see servants dismissed and tenant courts transferred to men who will show less mercy than I have shown. I see our land divided among strangers.”

“Mercy?” Elianor said. “Is that what you call it?”

His hand flattened against the ledger. “What would you have me do?”

She had no answer that could fit inside a room. Sell the silver, the paintings, the hunting horses. Open the stores. Refuse the lenders and accept the consequences.

But she knew what would happen. Their neighbors would circle Greyfen like crows. The courts favored those with money, and the Veys had very little left.

Alric closed the ledger.

“There is one course left to us,” he said.

Elianor felt the chill before he spoke.

“No.”

“You do not yet know what I mean.”

“I know.”

“The Arbridge family has offered to settle the greater part of our debts.”

“In exchange for marriage.”

His gaze shifted to the window. “Yes.”

Lord Caelan Arbridge was thirty-two, wealthy beyond measure, and heir to the largest ironworks in the western counties. He had a polished manner, a long memory, and no reputation for generosity except where generosity purchased something. Elianor had met him twice at court. The first time he kissed her hand and asked whether she preferred the sea or mountains. The second, he remembered her answer and told her that Arbridge possessed a summer house overlooking the sea.

She had not thought he remembered because he had listened. She had thought he remembered because he noticed everything that might one day belong to him.

“How much?” she asked.

“Enough to pay the Harrowmere lenders. Enough to restore the roof and keep the stores open through spring. Enough that the creditors will no longer have cause to take the estate.”

“And what does he receive?”

“An alliance with House Vey.”

“That is what you call me?”

His expression tightened. “I call you my daughter.”

“Then say what he receives.”

Alric was silent.

The answer lay between them: Greyfen, its lands, its tenants, its servants, its history. Her hand in his, and through hers the right to enter every locked room and command every life beneath its roof.

“Caelan would take control of the debts.”

“He would assume responsibility for them.”

“He would take control of Greyfen.”

“Eventually, yes. But the Vey name would remain.”

“On the gate.”

“On the gate,” Alric said bitterly. “In the chapel. In the records. In the line of succession, if you bear a son.”

Elianor looked at him. “And if I refuse?”

He did not answer at once.

Outside, somewhere below the library, a servant dropped a tray. The crash rang through the house, followed by hurried apologies and the butler’s sharp voice.

“If you refuse,” Alric said, “the notes may be called. The estate will be sold. The tenants will be displaced. Those who have served us will scatter. I will be ruined.”

“You speak as if my marriage is a remedy for everyone’s suffering.”

“It may be the only remedy left.”

“It is a sacrifice.”

“Yes.”

The word was so plain that she almost wished he had lied.

His eyes shone, though whether with grief or exhaustion she could not tell. “I would not ask it if there were another way.”

“You have not looked for another way.”

“I have looked until there was nothing left to look at.”

“Then look at me.”

He did.

Elianor wanted him to say that she was free. She wanted him to tear the ledger in half, summon the horses, and tell the creditors to take what they could carry. She wanted him to be a father before he was Lord Vey.

Instead, he said, “Caelan comes next week.”

Her throat tightened. “To discuss the terms?”

“To make the arrangement formal.”

“Have you already agreed?”

“I have agreed to hear him.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Alric’s silence was answer enough.

Elianor crossed to the window. Rain blurred the village until the cottages became smudges of brown beneath the hill. Somewhere down there, a family slept beneath canvas. Somewhere in the kitchens, servants burned chairs to warm rooms no one had the courage to abandon.

She had been raised to believe that privilege was a duty. A lady was a shelter, a bridge, a keeper of the family’s honor. She endured what others could not because her endurance spared them.

But if her endurance bound her to a man who would own the house, the land, and every person beneath its roof, what had she spared them?

“Will he leave the servants in their places?” she asked.

“If the household proves useful.”

“And the tenants?”

“Those who meet their obligations will remain.”

“Obligations he will define.”

Alric looked away.

Elianor pressed her palm to the cold glass. Beyond it, the hill descended into rain. Greyfen’s walls rose behind her, enclosing her in stone, duty, and the accumulated hunger of generations.

“Send for him,” she said.

Her father’s head lifted. “Elianor—”

“Send for Lord Caelan Arbridge.”

The words seemed to fasten themselves to everything within the room.

Alric came toward her. “You do not have to decide tonight.”

“You have already decided for me.”

“I am trying to save you.”

“No,” she said softly. “You are trying to save House Vey.”

He stopped.

For a long moment neither moved. Then Alric bowed his head, not as a lord to his daughter, but as a defeated man before the only judgment he could no longer evade.

In the courtyard below, rain gathered in the worn grooves between the stones. It ran beneath the gates and down the hill toward the village, carrying ash, mud, and the thin remnants of the house’s strength into the dark.

By spring, Elianor thought, Greyfen would belong to Caelan Arbridge.

She did not yet know what would become of her.

Only that the door had closed, and she was standing on the wrong side of it.

chapters.name: A Favorable Match
chapters.content:
## A Favorable Match

By the time Lord Caelan Arbridge arrived, rain had settled over Greyfen like a second roof.

It drummed on the slate and streamed from the gutters, turning the courtyard to black mud. Servants crossed the entrance hall carrying lamps and trays, leaving damp prints on the flagstones. Everyone had been instructed to look untroubled.

Sella fastened the last pearl at Elianor’s throat.

“Too tight?” Elianor asked.

“No, my lady.”

“You look ill.”

“I am only tired.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Sella attempted a smile. “The kitchen maid says it is something I ate. The cook says it is the weather. I say it will pass if everyone stops asking me about it.”

“You should be in bed.”

“And leave you to face a rich lord alone? He might think Greyfen had no servants.”

“He will think Greyfen has too many.”

Sella’s expression sharpened, but she lowered her eyes. Among the household, jokes about the estate were safest when spoken softly.

Elianor looked at herself in the mirror. Her gown was blue-gray silk, old but carefully brushed, embroidered at the sleeves with the Vey hawk. The pearls had belonged to her grandmother. Everything she wore was inherited, repaired, or borrowed against.

A favorable match, her father had called it.

Below, the great doors opened. Cold air swept through the hall, carrying the smell of horses and rain.

“He has arrived,” Sella said.

Elianor descended with her hands folded before her. Lord Alric waited at the foot of the stairs in a dark green coat whose cuff was frayed. Beside him stood the steward, the housekeeper, and several older servants chosen to represent Greyfen’s dignity.

Caelan Arbridge entered without haste.

He was not handsome in the careless way of young men who had never been denied anything. His features were narrow and composed, his black hair cut close at the temples, his eyes a clear gray that seemed to measure every object they rested upon. His traveling cloak was the color of wet stone. Not one drop remained upon him.

He removed his gloves finger by finger.

“Lord Vey,” he said, offering his hand. “I am grateful for your welcome, especially in such weather.”

“My lord, Greyfen is honored.”

Caelan’s gaze moved to Elianor.

“Lady Elianor.”

“My lord.”

He bowed over her hand without touching it with his lips.

“I have heard that Valedorn is beautiful in every season,” he said.

“People say that when they are trying to sell it.”

A pause passed between them. Then Caelan smiled.

“Then I shall be careful whom I believe.”

Alric laughed too quickly. “The road must have been intolerable. We feared the bridge at Harth Fen would be impassable.”

“It nearly was.” Caelan glanced toward the windows, where rain ran in wavering lines down the glass. “Though I confess I am less accustomed to houses that have not yet been repaired.”

The steward stiffened. Alric pretended not to hear.

“We have arranged rooms for you,” he said. “Dinner will be served in an hour.”

“I hope you will permit us to discuss my visit first. I prefer to dine without uncertainty.”

He spoke as if uncertainty were a stain to be removed by a servant.

The library fire had been built high. Maps covered one table; ledgers covered another. Caelan’s solicitor, a thin man named Varr, arranged documents before him while an Arbridge servant poured wine.

Elianor sat beside her father. Caelan took the chair opposite, with the fire at his back.

Varr cleared his throat.

“By the terms proposed, Lord Arbridge will discharge the immediate obligations owed by House Vey to the Harrowmere lenders, Kestrel Bank, and the Crown’s timber office. He will also assume the notes held against Greyfen mill and the north silver tract.”

Alric’s hand tightened on the arm of his chair.

“In return,” Caelan said, “Lady Elianor will enter marriage with me before the first day of spring.”

The words altered the air.

Elianor kept her gaze on the papers. “And the estate?”

“Greyfen remains in your father’s name until his death.”

“Remains,” she repeated. “Yet you assume the debts.”

“I assume responsibility for them.”

“Which is not the same thing.”

“No,” he said. “It is more serious.”

Varr pushed a document toward her. “The agreement grants Lord Arbridge full authority to direct Greyfen’s financial administration until the debts are settled. This includes appointing a steward, revising rents, altering labor obligations, and disposing of timber or mineral rights as necessary.”

Elianor did not touch the paper. “And the household?”

Caelan leaned back. “The household will be placed under my protection.”

“Protection from what?”

“From uncertainty. From creditors. From the consequences of a failing estate.”

“The servants are not creditors.”

“No. But they depend upon the estate’s survival. If Greyfen is seized, what do you imagine will become of them?”

It was her father’s argument, dressed in finer words.

Caelan continued. “I have no wish to dismiss loyal people. But loyalty does not excuse inefficiency. A household of this size cannot be maintained for sentiment. Those who remain must serve where they are needed.”

There it was: not cruelty, but certainty. He did not speak of people as though they were beneath him. He spoke as though they were pieces on a board whose proper placement he alone understood.

“And the tenants?” Elianor asked.

“The same principle applies.”

“Even when the harvest fails?”

“Especially then. A failed harvest is no argument for allowing an estate to fail as well.”

Her anger rose, familiar and helpless. “What happens to families who cannot meet their rent or labor demands?”

“Eviction is a last resort.”

“My lord, it happened last week.”

Alric’s head lifted. “Elianor.”

“The south cottage family was turned out in the rain. Their youngest child was ill.”

Caelan’s gaze shifted to her father, then back. “I regret that the matter was handled without your knowledge.”

“Do you?”

“I regret any disorder in Greyfen’s management. Once we are married, such matters will be reviewed before action is taken.”

He would not prevent the eviction. He would ensure she could not be kept ignorant of it.

A log broke in the grate.

Caelan folded his hands. “I understand that you have compassion, Lady Elianor. It is a quality much praised in a wife. But compassion must be governed by judgment.”

“And judgment by whom?”

“By the person accountable for the consequences.”

His eyes held hers.

Elianor set down the agreement. “I would like to speak with my father.”

Caelan rose at once. “Of course.”

The courtesy was flawless. It did not conceal that he had granted permission.

Alric led her through the adjoining passage to his study. He closed the door and glanced toward the library as if Caelan might hear through the wood.

“You challenged him too directly,” he said.

“He intends to control every part of Greyfen.”

“He intends to save it.”

“He intends to own it.”

“He already owns the debts.”

Alric crossed to the window. Rain had erased the lawns and gardens, leaving only a blur of trees. His reflection hovered in the glass: an old man wearing a younger man’s coat.

“You think I do not know what this costs?” he asked.

“I think you know what it costs the house.”

His jaw tightened.

“Your mother left this estate with forty-three tenant families, twelve household servants, and a debt no larger than the value of the east pasture. I have watched all of it diminish. Roofs fail. Roads wash out. The mill stands idle half the year. The lenders do not care whether a child is ill in a cottage. They care whether the note is paid.”

“Then let Greyfen go.”

He turned sharply. “And send every servant into the road? Let creditors divide the land? Let Arbridge take the mill, timber, and cottages? You speak as though surrender is mercy.”

“It may be more merciful than this.”

“Your uncle said the same before selling his southern fields. The tenants there were scattered within a year. Half became laborers in the ironworks. The rest crossed the border.”

Elianor remembered the family from the south cottage, the mother clutching blankets around her coughing child.

“And marrying me to Caelan prevents that?”

“It gives us time.”

“It gives him authority.”

“It gives us protection.”

“For how long?”

“As long as it takes to restore the estate.”

She laughed without humor. “You cannot restore what you have already surrendered.”

Alric came toward her. “I know what I ask of you.”

“Do you know what he is asking?”

“He is offering you a secure position, a household of your own, and a husband with reason to preserve what belongs to you.”

“What belongs to me?”

“Greyfen.”

“No. Greyfen belongs to House Vey. I belong to House Vey. That is the whole problem.”

His expression faltered.

“If I agree,” she said, “you will guarantee that no servant is dismissed or transferred without my consent.”

Alric hesitated.

“You cannot even promise that.”

“I can promise to negotiate.”

“You are already negotiating me.”

“Elianor—”

“No.” She stepped back. “If this marriage is to save Greyfen, I want it written that the household remains under my authority.”

“Caelan will not accept that.”

“Then he is not offering protection. He is purchasing the right to command.”

Alric closed his eyes. “You cannot win every condition.”

“I know.”

The rain struck the window.

At last she said, “Send for him.”

Her father opened his eyes.

“Send for Lord Arbridge. Tell him I accept the match.”

Relief moved across his face, and she hated him for it. He reached for her hand, but she withdrew it.

“Do not mistake this for happiness,” she said.

“I do not.”

“No. You mistake it for rescue.”

She left him in the study.

In the library, Caelan stood beside the fire, speaking quietly with Varr. He turned when she entered.

“My lady.”

“I will accept your proposal.”

His expression warmed by a fraction. Not joy. Satisfaction.

“I am honored.”

“I will require provisions.”

“I expected as much.”

“The household servants are not to be dismissed or transferred without my consent.”

“Until the debts are settled.”

“Until I release them from service.”

Caelan considered her. “You have a generous heart.”

“I have made a condition.”

“Very well. Until you release them, provided their conduct remains satisfactory and the estate can support their wages.”

“Wages are not the only measure of necessity.”

“Then we shall discuss necessity when it arises.”

It was not an agreement. It was a door left open for him to close later.

“The tenants are to receive reasonable terms in years of failed harvest,” she said.

“Reasonable according to whom?”

“According to the harvest.”

“I will consult the steward.”

“You will consult me.”

For the first time, something hard showed beneath his courtesy.

“Once we are married, Lady Elianor, Greyfen will require a single authority.”

“Then you should have proposed to the estate rather than to me.”

Varr lowered his eyes. Caelan’s mouth curved, though his gaze remained cold.

“You will find that marriage is a partnership. Partnerships fail when both parties attempt to command.”

“And succeed when one does?”

“When one is accountable.”

She understood then that he did not see himself as a villain. He would call every restriction prudence, every seizure stewardship, every silenced objection the necessary cost of order. He would be courteous while closing his hand around the house.

Caelan extended his hand.

“Then let us begin with trust.”

She placed her fingers in his.

His hand was warm, dry, and firm. He held hers a moment longer than etiquette required, as if testing the weight of something newly acquired.

Elianor smiled. A lady’s composure was a kind of armor. It could conceal fear, anger, even the trembling of the body beneath silk.

“Let us begin,” she said.

Outside, rain fell upon Greyfen’s broken roofs, empty cottages, and dark fields. Inside, the agreement was carried to the desk, where the ink waited.

chapters.name: The Falconer’s Son
chapters.content:
The day after Elianor placed her hand in Lord Caelan Arbridge’s, Greyfen Manor seemed to have grown smaller.

Every passage led toward a future she had already agreed to enter. Servants lowered their voices when she passed. The steward’s clerk carried fresh sheets of parchment between the solar and library, each fold sealed with Arbridge’s black device. Sella was ill again behind her closed door, insisting that her unsettled stomach was nothing. A seamstress pinned Elianor’s sleeves and spoke of wedding silks as though silk could make a prison beautiful.

At midday, Elianor took her cloak from its peg and left without telling anyone where she was going.

The path behind Greyfen had once been used by hunting parties. It descended through a beechwood toward the old forester’s lodge, then disappeared into bracken and marsh grass. No one had maintained it in years. Fallen branches lay beneath the dripping canopy, and rain had carved narrow channels through the mud.

Elianor walked until the manor vanished behind the trees.

The woods did not care that she was Lady Elianor Vey. They had endured her father’s hounds, falcons, huntsmen, and axes without obedience. Here, no one asked her to smile at a stranger, sign a document, or promise that her marriage would preserve the past.

She was nearly past the lodge when she heard the bird cry.

It was a harsh, broken sound. Not the clear call of a hunting hawk, but a rasp of pain.

Elianor stopped and pushed open the crooked door.

A young man crouched beside the ruined hearth with his back to her. He wore a mud-stained wool coat and boots worn thin at the toes. A leather glove covered his left hand. On it lay a goshawk, its feathers puffed against the cold, one wing held at an unnatural angle.

The man turned. His hand closed around the knife at his belt.

“Go back,” he said.

“I heard the bird.”

“That does not make you welcome.”

Rain slipped from the edge of Elianor’s hood and tapped against the floorboards. She looked at the blood-darkened strip of linen around the goshawk’s wing.

“You need a surgeon.”

“I need clean bandages and a splint.”

“I can send for them.”

“No.”

The refusal was so immediate that she studied him more closely. He was perhaps her age or a little older, lean and weather-darkened, with black hair tied at the nape. He did not bow. He did not flatter her. His eyes moved from her gloves to the fine clasp at her throat and back again.

“Lady Vey,” he said.

“You know me.”

“I know the daughter of the man who owns these woods.”

“Then you know I can obtain medicine.”

“I know the manor surgeon treats men who pay him.”

“He treats the household.”

“And does the household include a falconer’s son?”

“If he is employed by Greyfen.”

“Employed,” he repeated. “That is a gracious word for being born where my father worked.”

The goshawk shifted weakly. He steadied it at once, murmuring beneath his breath until it settled.

“What is your name?” Elianor asked.

“Tomas Vale.”

“Your father is the head falconer.”

“Yes.”

She had seen him before, though only as a boy carrying meat to the mews or cleaning leather jesses. The realization embarrassed her. She knew the household accounts better than she knew the people who made the household function.

“What happened?”

“A trap.”

“Whose?”

His expression hardened. “A trap does not ask whether the creature who finds it is noble.”

Elianor stepped farther inside. The lodge held little besides a broken table, a pot, damp kindling, and a blanket spread over old crates. No fire burned. The bread on the table had been reduced to a heel.

“Let me help.”

“You came to the woods for something?”

“I came to walk.”

“People from the manor come here when they want something.”

“What could I want from you?”

“That is what I am waiting to learn.”

She should have been angry. Instead, she felt the futility of her position. In the lodge, her name could not mend a wing. Her command had no force unless she brought men to enforce it, and bringing men would mean taking the bird from Tomas.

“I can bring medicine tomorrow,” she said.

“I said no.”

“You may refuse it when I arrive.”

He stared at her, then looked down at the goshawk.

“Warmth,” he said reluctantly. “Clean water. No one touches the wing until I have splints.”

“I can bring willow.”

“I can find willow.”

“Food, then.”

“We have food.”

Elianor glanced at the empty pot.

“For the bird,” he added.

“Birds do not eat bread.”

“Neither do men, apparently.”

She looked at his hollow cheeks and the looseness of his coat. Beneath his suspicion, he was simply hungry.

“Do not mistake an offer for pity,” she said.

“Do not mistake pity for kindness.”

Elianor left him with the rain.

When she returned to Greyfen, a groom waited beneath the archway, anxious and reproachful. Her cloak was taken. Her boots were cleaned. A maid hurried toward her to say Lord Alric wished to see her in the solar.

Her father sat before the cold fireplace with the marriage agreement spread across his desk. The parchment was crowded with clauses concerning debts, rents, labor, timber, and authority.

“You must not wander alone,” he said.

“I was walking.”

“You are to be married. Caelan’s man arrives tomorrow to inspect the north accounts. You must be present.”

“I will be present.”

He looked at her as though attendance ought to be a comfort. “You accepted the match.”

“I did.”

“You cannot accept it only in name and refuse the obligations that follow.”

Elianor thought of Tomas’s question: What could I want from you?

“I know,” she said.

That night, wind pressed against her shutters, and rain dripped somewhere inside the walls. Twice she woke believing she heard the goshawk cry.

At dawn, before the seamstress could claim her, Elianor went to the kitchens.

Cook stared when she requested bread, salt meat, and a small jar of goose fat. Elianor took a warm roll and wrapped everything in a cloth. Then she went to the infirmary. The surgeon was absent, but his cabinet stood unlocked. She chose willow-bark tincture, honey, dried comfrey, and a length of clean linen.

The theft was small enough that no one would have called it theft if she had sent a servant. Taking the things herself made it feel like a decision.

The woods were pale beneath the morning clouds. Every branch held water. Elianor walked quickly, telling herself she returned because the goshawk needed care. She did not ask why the thought of finding Tomas there urged her forward.

He was outside the lodge, stripping bark from a young willow branch.

When he saw her, he rose.

“You came back.”

“You expected me not to?”

“I expected you to remember that people at Greyfen have better things to do than mend a bird.”

“I remembered that you had no clean bandages.”

His gaze fell to the bundle in her arms. Suspicion crossed his face, followed by something less guarded.

“I did not ask for these.”

“No.”

“Why bring them?”

“Because I chose to.”

He considered her, then moved aside. “Come in, then. If you are going to interfere, you may as well hold the lamp.”

There was no lamp, but she entered.

The goshawk lay beneath the blanket, its head turned toward them. Tomas had carved two smooth willow splints. Elianor set the food on the table and knelt beside the bird.

“You did well,” she said.

“I know.”

She glanced up.

“You asked.”

Despite herself, she nearly smiled. “You are very certain of yourself.”

“Not certain. Careful.”

He began unwrapping the soaked linen. The wound was swollen and angry. Elianor held the bird while he cleaned it. Its heart beat violently beneath her hands.

“It will bite you,” Tomas said.

“So will you, apparently.”

His hands paused, but he continued without answering.

When he finished setting the splints, he covered the goshawk’s eyes with a fold of cloth. Elianor reached for the roll, broke it in half, and offered him one piece.

He accepted it.

For a little while they ate in silence. The rain began again, soft against the broken roof.

“The south-cottage family was bitten worse than this,” Tomas said.

Elianor’s fingers tightened around the bread. “I know about them.”

“Do you?”

“A family was evicted after the failed harvest.”

“The father was ill. The youngest child had a fever. Their rent was raised, and they were ordered to work three days a week repairing roads that washed out each night.”

“I know.”

“And still the eviction happened.”

“My father approved it.”

“Your family did.”

“Yes.”

He tied off the bandage and looked at her. “That is a distinction nobles use when they want clean hands.”

“I am not using it.”

“Not yet.”

The words struck harder than an accusation because she had already feared they were true.

“I was born into the house that took their home,” she said. “I eat from stores their labor fills. I cannot pretend otherwise. But I did not choose the rent.”

“No. You inherited it.”

“Just as you inherited service.”

His jaw tightened.

“I did not mean—”

“Yes, you did.”

Neither spoke for a moment. Outside, water fell from the eaves. A thrush called somewhere beyond the clearing.

Elianor looked at the bird. “Will it fly again?”

“If the wing knits cleanly.”

“And if it does not?”

“Then it will live without flying.”

She heard the meaning beneath his answer. Some forms of survival were only different kinds of captivity.

Tomas tore the remaining bread in two and gave part to the goshawk. He ate the rest slowly.

“You are to marry Arbridge,” he said.

It was not a question.

“Yes.”

“Congratulations.”

The word was flat.

“Thank you.”

They looked at each other, each waiting for the other to admit the lie.

“Then you should not come here,” Tomas said.

“I know.”

“People will talk.”

“They already do.”

“And he will notice.”

“He notices everything.”

“Then why are you here?”

Elianor had no answer that would survive being spoken aloud. She reached toward the goshawk, stopping just before its feathers.

“Because it was hurt.”

Tomas watched her with an expression guarded enough to resemble indifference.

The lodge darkened as clouds gathered over the trees. Neither of them moved to leave.

chapters.name: Willow Splints
chapters.content:
## Willow Splints

The rain had stopped by dawn, but the woods kept it.

Water fell from the black branches, striking the leaves beneath Elianor’s boots and darkening her cloak. Mist lay low among the trees. Beyond it, Greyfen Manor was only a pale shape on the hill, its chimneys breathing thin smoke into the washed-out sky.

She had told Sella she meant to walk before breakfast. It was not precisely a lie. She had walked; she had simply gone farther than anyone would approve.

The forester’s lodge stood where the woods thickened, half-swallowed by ivy and bramble. One shutter hung loose from its hinge. Elianor lifted the latch and pushed open the door.

Tomas looked up from the pallet near the cold hearth. He had not slept much. The goshawk lay wrapped in a blanket across his knees, its hooked beak tucked toward its breast.

“You came back,” he said.

“You sound disappointed.”

“I sound surprised.”

“That is less flattering.”

“I was not trying to flatter you.”

She removed her cloak. Beneath it she wore a plain brown gown, chosen because no one at the manor would notice its absence. She had also brought a basket covered with linen.

Tomas’s eyes went to it. “What is that?”

“Food. Linen. Willow bark. Honey and comfrey.”

“I have food.”

“You have half a heel of bread and two onions.”

“That is food.”

“It is a poor argument for living.”

His mouth moved as though he nearly smiled, but the expression disappeared. “And the bird?”

“Still alive, I hope.”

“Better than yesterday.”

He shifted the goshawk carefully. Its wing had been bound against its body with strips of torn cloth, and one small bone pressed at an unnatural angle beneath the feathers.

“Tell me what you need me to do,” Elianor said.

Tomas glanced at the blackened pot near the hearth. “Boil water.”

She filled it from a bucket and set it over the fire. When the water trembled, Tomas carried the bird to the table and cut away the old bindings. The goshawk struggled once, violently, and he pressed one hand over its breast.

“Hold its head,” he said.

Elianor hesitated.

“Behind the beak. Gently.”

She placed her hands where he showed her. The bird’s heart hammered against her palm. Tomas worked with careful speed, lifting away the torn cloth. Beneath it, the flesh was swollen and livid.

Elianor drew breath through her teeth.

“Do not look at it like that,” Tomas said.

“Like what?”

“As though it is a crime.”

“Is it not?”

He stopped. The bird shuddered between them.

“It was caught in a trap,” he said. “A crime requires someone to answer for it.”

“Perhaps someone will.”

“Perhaps the trapper is dead. Perhaps he is a boy who set it because his family had eaten nothing since yesterday. Perhaps he owns the land and believes everything upon it belongs to him. There are many sorts of wickedness.”

Elianor kept her hands steady. “You do not know which kind this was.”

“No. I have seen enough of all of them.”

Tomas dipped a strip of linen into the hot water, wrung it out, and passed it to her. “Clean the wound.”

She touched the cloth to the wing. The goshawk snapped at the air. Tomas caught its head before it could reach her.

“Steady,” he murmured.

They worked without speaking. Elianor rinsed blood from the feathers while Tomas examined the break, feeling along the bone with his fingertips. His hands were roughened at the knuckles, but he touched the bird with extraordinary gentleness.

“Will it heal?” she asked.

“If the bone knits straight.”

“And if it does not?”

“It may live. It may never fly.”

The words settled between them.

Tomas took two thin lengths of willow from a bundle beside the hearth. He shaved them smooth with his knife, turning each strip beneath the blade until no splinter remained.

“Those are the splints?”

“They bend without breaking. A bone needs something beside it that knows how to give.”

He laid the splints along either side of the wing. Elianor held them in place while he bound linen around them. Their fingers met once. His hand was warm. Neither moved immediately.

Then he tightened the bandage.

The goshawk flinched.

“I am sorry,” Elianor whispered.

Tomas looked at her. “It cannot understand you.”

“No. But I do.”

“That may be worse.”

He tied the final knot, covered the bird, and carried it to a perch near the fire. Elianor poured water into two chipped cups. She had brought bread, hard cheese, and three apples. Tomas accepted the bread only after she took some herself.

“You will be missed,” he said.

“Not yet.”

“Your father knows you come here?”

“No.”

“Your maid?”

“No.”

“Then you are either very brave or very foolish.”

“I have been called both. Mostly by myself.”

He leaned against the table, holding the cup between both hands. The lodge was small and plain: rough boards patched with moss, a narrow bed, a cloak on a peg, dried herbs hanging beside the hearth. Nothing belonged there except by necessity.

Elianor envied it.

Tomas noticed. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You keep saying that.”

“It is useful.”

“For people who do not wish to answer.”

She broke off a piece of bread. “You ask many questions for a man who distrusts me.”

“I distrust most people.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is a warning.”

She turned the bread in her fingers. “My family evicted a man from the south cottages last month.”

Tomas said nothing.

“His wife was ill. Their youngest had a fever. They had missed the rent after the harvest failed, and the steward still required the father to work the road crews. My father signed the order.”

“Oren Vale,” Tomas said.

She looked at him.

“My mother knew his wife.”

Elianor lowered the bread.

“They were turned out in rain like this,” he continued. “A year ago. The cottage leaked, but it was better than the ditch. My mother had been coughing for months. We were given three days to leave.”

“I did not know.”

“You knew yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“And it did not stop the eviction.”

“No.”

He watched her. “You are waiting for me to forgive you.”

“I am not asking anything from you.”

“Most people who confess are.”

“I argued with my father,” she said. “He told me that if he spared one cottage, he would have to spare ten, and then the creditors would take the estate. He said the family would be scattered, servants dismissed, and tenants placed under a lord who would show less mercy.”

“Did you give the family money?”

“No.”

“Food?”

“No.”

“Did your father withdraw the order?”

“No.”

Tomas looked away. His silence was harder to bear than anger.

“I was not allowed to interfere,” she said.

“Not allowed?”

“I am his daughter.”

“You are a lady.”

“That is not the same as being free.”

He gave a short, humorless laugh. “You expect me to believe that?”

“I expect nothing from you. You think I have never been refused anything because I was born in a house with servants. You think silk is liberty. It is not.”

She stood, and the bench scraped against the floor.

“My father has chosen my marriage,” she continued. “The arrangements are already being made. I am to marry a man who purchased our debts and calls the purchase protection. I may ask that servants not be dismissed, but he decides whether they have behaved well enough to remain. I may ask that tenants receive time after a failed harvest, but he decides what time means. If I refuse, Greyfen may be seized. People who have done nothing wrong will lose their homes.”

“You can still refuse.”

“Yes.”

“Then you have a choice.”

Elianor met his eyes. “Do you?”

He did not answer.

The fire shifted. For a moment, the only sound was rainwater slipping from the eaves.

“My father has served House Vey since he was fourteen,” Tomas said. “He knows every mews, every hawk, every path where the rabbits run. If he leaves, he has nowhere to go. If he stays, he belongs to whoever owns Greyfen. That is the choice servants are given.”

He drank from his cup.

“My mother was ill when we were evicted. We slept in an empty sheep shed for two nights. My father carried her to a village beyond the marsh. She died there before winter ended.”

Elianor could not speak.

“I was twelve,” he said. “Old enough to understand the house had not killed her. Young enough to think that meant no one had.”

The lodge seemed to draw inward around them.

“I am sorry,” Elianor said.

Tomas’s eyes lifted. “Do not be sorry for what you did not do.”

“I am sorry for what my house did.”

“That is different.”

“Yes.”

He looked away first.

They listened to the fire and the dripping trees. Elianor finished her bread. Tomas ate half an apple, then placed the rest near the goshawk’s perch, though the bird did not stir.

“I cannot undo it,” she said.

“No.”

“But I can learn what happens before the orders reach the door.”

“That is not much.”

“It may be more than I have done.”

He considered this. “Why come here?”

“To treat the bird.”

“Why come back?”

She had no answer she could make respectable. The truth pressed against her ribs, embarrassing and insistent.

“Because yesterday you told me not to.”

“That is a poor reason.”

“It is the best one I have.”

He shook his head, but some tension left his shoulders.

Elianor rose before the household noticed her absence. Tomas rewrapped the goshawk and secured the cloth more carefully than before.

“You should not return,” he said.

“Because people will talk?”

“Because people notice what belongs to them.”

The words reminded her of Caelan, of the smooth hand laid over Greyfen’s accounts, of marriage described as an arrangement between houses while her own life disappeared beneath the ink.

“I do not belong to anyone,” she said.

Tomas met her eyes. “That is not what the world believes.”

She fastened her cloak. At the door, she turned back.

“The bird needs changing tomorrow.”

“I can manage.”

“I know.”

“Then why offer?”

She opened the door. Cold air entered, carrying the scent of wet earth.

“Because you may need help.”

“And if I do not?”

“Then you may refuse it.”

For the first time, his smile remained.

It was small, reluctant, and gone almost at once, but she carried it with her through the dripping trees.

The next morning, she would return. Not because the manor allowed it, nor because Tomas trusted her. The lodge was simply the only place in Valedorn where neither of them had yet been entirely named by someone else.

She stepped into the rain.

Behind her, the goshawk stirred beneath its wrappings, and Tomas began once more to watch over its broken wing.

chapters.name: The Shape of Rain
chapters.content:
## The Shape of Rain

By the fourth day, the goshawk had stopped trying to bite Tomas.

“This is progress,” Elianor said.

“It means she has decided I am the lesser danger.”

He glanced at her over the bird’s folded wing. Rain tapped against the roof of the forester’s lodge, finding its way through holes in the thatch and into bowls Tomas had placed beneath them. The air smelled of wet wool, old ash, and comfrey.

Elianor sat beside him on the floor, her skirts tucked beneath her knees. She had brought a basket from the kitchen, telling Cook it was for a tenant woman whose children were ill. The lie had been easy. Cook had pressed an extra loaf into the basket and murmured, “For the children, my lady.”

There were always children in need of bread at Greyfen.

Tomas unwound the linen from the goshawk’s wing. The swelling had diminished. The bones remained straight beneath the willow splints, and the wound was clean.

“She’ll keep the wing,” he said.

“And fly?”

“That depends on whether she wants to forgive the sky.”

His face was grave, but a brief smile touched his mouth.

Elianor opened the basket. “I brought cheese.”

“Then I forgive the sky.”

“And bread.”

“I forgive you.”

She handed him half the loaf. This time he accepted it without protest, though he divided the cheese with irritating precision.

“You might pretend to be grateful.”

“I am grateful.”

“You look as though I have handed you a legal document.”

“I have never eaten a legal document.”

“You have not eaten very much of anything at all, from what I can tell.”

“Have you been keeping account?”

“I was raised among ledgers.”

“That explains the suspicion.”

She threw a crust at him. He caught it.

For a while they ate in silence. It was no longer the strained silence of their first meetings. It held the rain, the bird’s quiet breathing, and the warmth of their shoulders nearly touching.

At Greyfen, time belonged to bells, meals, visitors, and obligations. Here, it belonged to weather and the needs of a wounded bird. Elianor had begun measuring her days by the hours between seeing Tomas.

She shivered.

He noticed at once. Without speaking, he drew off his cloak and held it out.

“I am not cold.”

“You are shaking.”

“The lodge is shaking for me.”

He settled the cloak around her shoulders. It smelled of pine smoke and hawk feathers. For a moment his hands remained near her throat.

Neither moved.

Then he stepped away and crouched beside the goshawk.

“You have a talent for making a person feel like a badly wrapped parcel,” Elianor said.

“I have never wrapped a parcel.”

“That is obvious.”

His reluctant smile hurt her with its gentleness.

She had seen handsome men all her life: neighboring lords, officers at winter suppers, polished heirs who discussed horses and politics while searching beyond her for the next advantageous match. Their beauty seemed separate from them, like a fine coat.

Tomas’s face was weathered, marked by a thin scar near his temple. His hands were rough and scarred. Yet when he touched the bird, every hard line in him softened.

“Who taught you?” she asked.

“To care for hawks?”

“To care for anything.”

His hands paused.

“My father,” he said. “Though he would say the birds taught me. He took me into the mews when I was six. By eight, I could tell a kestrel from a merlin by its cry. By ten, I could clean a wound.”

“And by twelve?”

He wrapped the goshawk’s wing and placed her in the straw-lined crate.

“By twelve, I learned a family could be turned out of a cottage even when the rent had been paid.”

Rain filled the pause.

“I am sorry,” Elianor said.

“Do not say it because it is expected.”

“I am saying it because it is true.”

“You were not there.”

“No.”

“You did not sign the order.”

“No.”

“But your father did.”

She met his eyes. “Yes.”

He seemed almost disappointed that she had not defended herself. “You say that plainly.”

“It is plain.”

“That does not make it bearable.”

“I know.”

“My mother was ill when we were put out. My father had worked two extra weeks on the south road, but the labor was counted against the rent, not toward it. We spent two nights in a sheep shed. She had a fever. There was no doctor. We left before dawn because the owner wanted the shed cleared for lambing.”

His voice remained controlled, but the control seemed costly.

“My father carried her until he could not. She died three days later in a village beyond the marsh.”

Elianor looked down at the cloak gathered in her hands.

“I did not know.”

“You were not meant to.”

“No. I was meant to know only that the cottage was reclaimed.”

“Reclaimed.” He repeated the word without anger. “A clean word.”

“Most clean words hide dirty work.”

His gaze sharpened. “And what will you do with what you know?”

She had no answer that would satisfy him.

“I do not know yet.”

“That is honest.”

“It is not sufficient.”

“No.”

He leaned back against the wall. “My father served House Vey from fourteen. He remains because he has nowhere else to go. Servants are offered the choice of belonging to whoever owns Greyfen or having nowhere to belong.”

“My father says that if we reduce the rents, the creditors will seize everything. The servants will lose employment. The tenants will be scattered. He says each cruelty prevents a greater one.”

“And do you believe him?”

“I believe he is afraid.”

“That was not my question.”

She watched rain slide down the warped window. “I believe the debts are real. I believe Greyfen may be taken. I believe people will suffer if it is.”

“And because the danger is real, every choice becomes righteous?”

“No.”

“But you accepted Caelan.”

The words struck deeper than she expected.

“I accepted the marriage,” she said.

“You think the distinction will comfort those who serve him?”

“It may give me authority to protect them.”

“Authority over what? Whether they are dismissed? Whether their labor is affordable? Whether his steward decides their hunger is inefficient?”

“I demanded protections.”

“And he granted them?”

“He agreed to consider them.”

Tomas laughed once, without humor. “Then Greyfen is saved.”

She rose too quickly, anger warming her face. “I am trying to keep people from being crushed.”

“And he knows it. That is why he can use them to hold you still.”

“You speak as though I am free to walk away.”

“You are.”

“My father’s debts will not vanish because I refuse a husband.”

“No.”

“The tenants will not become safe because I choose my happiness.”

“No.”

“The servants will not eat my principles.”

“No.” His voice sharpened. “But you can choose. You can choose badly and be condemned for it. I have had men tell me all my life that employment is a choice. It is not a choice when the other road is a ditch.”

“And you think I do not understand that?”

“I think you understand it from inside a warm house.”

The cruelty of it hurt because it was not wholly false.

“Then perhaps you should stop letting me into your cold one.”

His expression closed.

“I did not invite you.”

“No. You only gave me a reason to return.”

The goshawk shifted in her crate. Tomas reached down to steady it, his hand immediately gentle.

“I am not asking you to pity me,” he said.

“I do not pity you.”

“What, then?”

She had no answer that did not seem too large.

“I do not know.”

The words softened the space between them, though they did not mend it.

From beyond the trees came the faint clop of hooves.

Tomas turned toward the door. “Behind the wall. Now.”

“What?”

He crossed to the rear of the lodge, where rotting boards leaned against the wall. Behind them was a narrow recess.

“There is no room.”

“There is if you stop arguing.”

He pulled her into it just as the hoofbeats drew nearer. Tomas turned sideways, shielding her with his body. His shoulder pressed against her breastbone; one hand braced beside her head.

Outside, a voice called, “Tomas?”

Elianor held her breath.

The latch shifted.

A groom’s boots appeared through a gap in the boards, mud shining on the leather. He stepped inside.

“Vale, are you in there?”

The goshawk hissed.

“Damn bird.”

Tomas’s fingers closed around Elianor’s hand. His palm was rough and hot. She felt his pulse against her skin.

The groom moved closer. If they were discovered, no explanation could preserve either of them. She would be confined and married under watch. Tomas might be dismissed, arrested, or worse. Every servant who had helped her would pay for the secret.

The groom bent. His shadow crossed the floor.

Then a horse screamed outside, startling itself against its tether.

The groom swore and hurried back through the doorway. “Come on, you fool. I have no time for this.”

The door slammed. Hoofbeats receded through the trees.

Neither moved.

At last Tomas exhaled. His breath warmed her cheek. She became aware of the narrowness of the recess, his hand around hers, the way her face had turned toward his. If she lifted her chin, their mouths would touch.

He looked down at her.

The danger had not passed. It had only moved farther away.

“Go,” he whispered.

She should have agreed. Instead she asked, “Tomorrow?”

His eyes closed briefly.

“Tomorrow.”

He released her hand and stepped away. The sudden space between them felt colder than the rain.

Elianor took back her own cloak, but his remained around her shoulders.

“You have my cloak,” he said.

“I know.”

“Bring it back.”

“I may forget.”

“You keep accounts.”

She smiled despite herself. At the door, she looked once more toward the goshawk. The bird watched her with a hard, shining eye.

Then Elianor stepped into the rain.

The woods closed around her, dripping and secretive. Behind her, Tomas stood in the doorway until the trees hid him from sight. She walked toward Greyfen with his warmth clinging to her and understood that their refuge had never been safe.

It had only felt safe because, for a little while, they had been there together.

chapters.name: The First Flight
chapters.content:
The rain stopped before dawn.

Every branch in the woods carried a trembling weight of water, and mist lay low among the ferns. From the manor, Greyfen’s chimneys showed through the pale morning like broken teeth.

Elianor waited until Sella had fallen asleep again. Her maid had been restless through the night, turning beneath the blankets, her face damp with fever or some illness she would not name. Elianor left willow-bark tea beside the bed, then dressed in a plain wool gown and boots. She concealed Tomas’s cloak beneath her own.

She had not returned it.

The thought made her smile despite herself.

She crossed the servant stair, passed the kitchen where fires were being coaxed awake, and slipped through the side door. Cold touched her cheeks. Behind her, the manor stirred with pails, coughs, and shouted orders.

Then she entered the woods.

The forester’s lodge looked less abandoned in the morning. Water shone on its sagging roof, and a thin plume of smoke rose from the chimney. Tomas stood in the doorway, watching the path.

“You came,” he said.

“You sound surprised.”

“I was deciding whether to be offended.”

“That would have been a waste of your morning.”

His gaze settled on her face, then on the edge of his cloak showing beneath hers.

“You still have that.”

“I forgot.”

“You have forgotten it every day since I lent it to you.”

“Then it must be a serious condition.”

“There may be no cure.”

He stepped aside. The lodge smelled of smoke, wet wool, and crushed herbs. Near the hearth, the goshawk stood upon its perch, one foot clenched around the leather jess. The splints had been removed two days earlier. Its feathers were no longer dull, and the repaired wing lay close against its body, uneven but firm.

Elianor approached.

The bird regarded her with one bright, severe eye.

“She’s been restless since sunrise,” Tomas said. “Trying to climb the walls.”

“She may have grown tired of your company.”

“She has excellent judgment, then.”

Elianor smiled. “You think she is ready?”

“I think she believes she is ready. That is not the same thing.”

“Is that how you feel?”

The question escaped before she could soften it. Tomas looked at her, then turned back to the bird.

“She has to find out for herself.”

He carried the perch outside. Elianor followed. At the edge of a clearing, he set the goshawk upon a fallen oak and withdrew several paces.

For a moment, nothing happened.

The bird ruffled its feathers, lifted the injured wing, and folded it again. Tomas watched without blinking.

“Perhaps she has reconsidered,” Elianor whispered.

“Perhaps she is waiting for an audience to stop staring.”

The goshawk crouched.

Its wings opened.

Elianor’s breath caught. The bird sprang from the trunk, beating hard against the damp air. For one terrible instant it dropped, the injured wing lagging behind the other. Tomas stepped forward, but the goshawk twisted and caught a current rising from the clearing.

It climbed.

Not far, and not beautifully. Its flight was crooked and laboring, but fierce. It passed between two birches and landed heavily on a low branch.

Tomas exhaled.

Elianor laughed. The sound broke from her like a bell.

“She did it.”

“She nearly fell.”

“But she did not.”

Tomas whistled softly. The bird shifted along the branch, then launched again.

This time the flight was steadier. The goshawk crossed the clearing and vanished among the higher branches. They heard the rush of wings, then nothing.

“Where did she go?” Elianor asked.

“Somewhere she has chosen.”

“She may not come back.”

“No.”

There was no grief in the word, or grief so deep it had become calm.

Elianor looked toward the open sky. “She is fortunate. No one can tell her where to go.”

“Most birds would disagree.”

“Most birds have not met Lord Caelan Arbridge.”

Tomas’s expression tightened. “You should not speak of him here.”

“Does the forest report to him?”

“No. Men do.”

His gaze went toward the trees. He had been more guarded since yesterday, since the groom’s search had nearly uncovered them in the lodge.

“They were looking for you,” Elianor said.

“They were looking for a horse.”

“They knew your name.”

“Many people know my name.”

“Not many search abandoned lodges for you.”

His jaw tightened. “You should not come here again.”

The words struck harder than she expected. “Is that what you wanted to tell me?”

“It is what I should tell you.”

“Those are not the same thing.”

“No.”

He looked at her then, and she saw his fear—not of her, but of what discovery would bring.

“You nearly cried out yesterday,” he said. “They would have found you.”

“I did not.”

“I felt your hand shaking.”

“You were holding it.”

“Because you were about to make a sound.”

“I was not.”

“You were.” His voice sharpened. “You cannot keep coming here. If they discover you, they will lock you in a room and call it protection. They will send you to Caelan before you can breathe. They will dismiss my father, accuse him of theft, and put me in a cell—or worse.”

“I know.”

“Then do not make me say it again.”

She stepped closer. “You are asking me to leave.”

“I am asking you to live.”

“And what will you do?”

“Stay here. Work. Keep my head down.”

“That is not living.”

“It is what people like me are given.”

“You said choice existed for me.”

“It does.”

“Then it exists for you.”

He laughed without humor. “You think a man can walk away from service because a lady tells him to? My father has spent thirty years tied to this house. He has no land, no savings, no trade Greyfen has not claimed. If I run, he pays for it.”

“And if I marry Caelan?”

“Then you will pay for it.”

She flinched.

Tomas’s expression softened, but he did not take back the words. “I know why you agreed. You mean to protect them. But men like Caelan make use of every sacrifice placed before them. They do not become merciful because someone has suffered politely.”

“I know what he is.”

“Do you?”

The question opened something raw.

“I know enough,” she said. “I know he will control the accounts, alter the rents and labor demands, and call dismissal protection if it saves him wages. I know my father has given him Greyfen one promise at a time.”

“Then why marry him?”

“Because when those promises are called in, it will not be Caelan who sleeps beneath a leaking roof. It will be the tenants. Your father. The kitchen girls. Sella.” Her voice shook. “You speak as though refusing him leaves me free. It leaves hundreds of people facing a man who will seize everything without pretending to care.”

“And marrying him stops that?”

“No.”

“Then what does it do?”

She had no answer that would satisfy him. Only the hope that, inside the cage, she might loosen its bars for someone else.

Tomas looked at her with such sorrow that she wished he would be angry.

“I cannot make you choose me,” he said.

“I have not asked you to.”

“You have come here every day. You wear my cloak. You look at me as though—”

“As though what?”

He took one step toward her. “As though you have already chosen.”

Her heart struck hard against her ribs.

“I have chosen,” she said. “I simply have not chosen a life I can keep.”

For a moment neither moved.

Then Tomas reached for her.

His hand came to her cheek, roughened by work and warm from the fire. He paused, giving her time to turn away.

She did not.

His mouth touched hers, uncertainly at first. He withdrew, then returned with a tenderness so careful it broke her heart. Elianor caught his coat and pulled him closer.

The kiss deepened.

Rainwater fell from the branches around them. His hand slid behind her neck. She rose onto her toes to meet him, and all the things she had not dared to say passed between them: I am afraid. I am yours. I cannot promise tomorrow. Do not ask me to leave.

When they parted, their foreheads remained together.

“This cannot become respectable,” Tomas whispered.

“No.”

“There is no priest who can bless it into safety.”

“No.”

“No secret vow that will make them forgive us.”

“I know.”

He closed his eyes. “Then what are we doing?”

Elianor rested her hand over his. “Telling the truth, perhaps. For once.”

“The truth will kill us.”

“Not today.”

“Do not say that as though today is enough.”

“It is what we have.”

He kissed her again, with a hunger that frightened and delighted her. She held him until the cold returned and the forest brightened.

Above them, the goshawk called.

They looked up. The bird circled high between the bare branches, one wing still slightly lower than the other, then vanished toward the ridge.

“She will return when she is ready,” Tomas said.

Elianor looked at him. “Will you?”

His expression turned grave. “I will be here tomorrow.”

That was not what she had asked. It was the only answer he could give.

At last she left.

The path back to Greyfen seemed shorter than before. Her lips still tingled. She walked through wet ferns with her hands clasped before her, as though composure might contain the wildness moving through her.

At the manor, the bells had begun.

A footman intercepted her and said Lord Alric wished to see her in the accounting room. Elianor removed Tomas’s cloak beneath her own and folded it over her arm. She could not bring herself to put it away.

Her father stood over the ledgers with Caelan’s seal beside them. He spoke of Harrowmere, timber rights, and the need for an answer before the week ended. Elianor listened, nodded when required, and corrected two figures in the margin.

Beneath the table, her fingers pressed against the cloak’s worn fastening.

She carried the memory of Tomas’s mouth through every room.

When Caelan arrived at noon, she met him in the west parlor. He complimented the rain, the accounts, and her appearance with equal insincerity. He took her hand and held it a moment longer than courtesy required.
