“I will not do it,” he said.

Mara was quiet.

“I will not become an assassin because frightened men have decided one death might purchase them a better future.”

“Frightened men are often the first to understand the price of waiting.”

“I know the price.”

“Do you?”

He faced her. “My mother died because a landlord decided an empty cottage was worth more than a family. My father has given Greyfen forty years and owns nothing but the coat on his back. I know exactly what these men cost.”

“Then why speak as if the choice is between murder and innocence?”

“Because there is another choice.”

“Which is?”

“Take the records. Expose them. Make the tenants stand together. Force the courts to hear what they have done.”

Mara gave a short, weary laugh. “The courts are fed by the same tables. The judges borrow from the same banks. The Crown wants timber, silver, taxes, and quiet. You think a ledger will frighten them?”

“It may frighten the men who signed it.”

“It will frighten them enough to make them kill whoever carries it.”

His hand went instinctively to the waxed bundle under his shirt.

Mara saw the movement. Her eyes dropped, then returned to his face.

“You brought something back.”

“Copies.”

“From Southmere?”

“Labor rolls. Two sets. What tenants owed and what they paid.”

For the first time that morning, her certainty faltered. She reached for him, but he stepped back.

“Elianor must see them,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I should have told her.”

“Yes.”

The plainness of the answer hurt more than accusation.

“She cannot know everything,” he said, though the defense sounded feeble even to him. “If Caelan searches her rooms—”

“Then she may choose whether to hide them, burn them, or use them. That is what choice means.”

Tomas closed his eyes.

He saw Elianor again, not in the gallery but in the lodge, kneeling beside the injured goshawk with blood on her fingertips. She had listened when he told her what happened to his mother. She had not asked forgiveness for a thing she had not done. She had simply listened, as if the truth were an obligation rather than a wound to be politely acknowledged.

And then he had lied to her.

The door shuddered in its frame as a gust struck it.

Mara gathered her cloak. “The gathering will be held at Greyfen.”

“When?”

“Three nights from now, perhaps four. The message was sent yesterday. Caelan wants the roads watched before the lords arrive.”

“You expect me to enter a hall surrounded by guards and put a knife in him?”

“I expect you to understand why men are asking.”

“No.”

“Not even if his death delays the raids?”

“No.”

“Not even if it saves Elianor from being taken into his household?”

The answer caught in him.

Mara studied his face. “There it is.”

“I said no.”

“You said it as if the word were a stone you could hold between your teeth.”

He turned on her. “You think killing him saves her? It makes her a widow before she is a wife, a traitor’s accomplice, and the daughter of a house whose servants will be punished for her. If I fail, I hang. If I succeed, the estate burns. You know that.”

“I know all of it.”

“Then stop asking.”

“I am not asking you to be brave,” Mara said. “I am asking whether your refusal comes from principle or fear.”

He could not answer.

The distinction had been clean when she first entered: murder was wrong, resistance was necessary, and he would not let necessity make him into the thing he hated. But now the lines blurred. Caelan’s seal lay between them. Names and dates and orders. A future in which men came through the rain to Greyfen and dragged servants from their beds. A future in which Elianor stood beside Caelan while he called seizure protection.

Perhaps refusing to kill was courage.

Perhaps it was merely the luxury of someone who had not yet been forced to choose whose blood mattered.

Mara opened the door.

“Tomas.”

He looked at her.

“If you will not kill him, then do not mistake that for the end of your decision. The gathering will still come. The raids will still come. And Caelan will still take Elianor.”

She stepped into the rain, then paused beneath the eave.

“Bring her the records,” she said. “Tell her the truth before someone else decides what she is allowed to know.”

Then she was gone.

Tomas remained in the ruined lodge until the cold reached through his boots. At last he removed the waxed packet from beneath his shirt and set it on the table beside Caelan’s order.

Two kinds of evidence. One might expose a system. The other might end a man.

He thought of Elianor’s hand lifting in the gallery after the betrothal, a small movement toward him before he turned away. He had believed then that he was protecting her from the danger of his love.

Now he understood that he had only left her alone with it.

Outside, a hawk cried from somewhere beyond the ridge.

Tomas looked toward the sound, but the rain concealed the bird. He picked up the records and held them against his chest, uncertain whether restraint was the first act of mercy or the first form of cowardice.

Then he stepped into the weather and began the road back to Greyfen.

chapters.name: A Bargain with Winter
chapters.content:
### A Bargain with Winter

By the eleventh day of rain, Greyfen smelled of wet wool, extinguished fires, and earth forced through the cracks in its foundations.

Water ran down the western stair. Bowls stood beneath leaks in the blue salon, overflowing faster than servants could empty them. In the lower yard, carts sat axle-deep in mud. The road to the timber tract had become a brown river, and every hour without repair brought the Crown’s license closer to forfeiture.

Elianor sat in her father’s study with the marriage articles before her.

The parchment promised that no servant of Greyfen would be dismissed without cause. It promised that tenants would retain their leases so long as rents were paid. It promised that Tomas and Oren Vale would remain in falconry.

All the things Caelan had permitted her to ask for.

All the things he had made her understand could be withdrawn.

Her father stood by the window, one hand against the stone frame. Rain obscured the glass, turning his reflection into a wavering ghost.

“You could still ask for more,” Alric said.

“Could I?”

“The terms may be amended.”

“By whom?”

He turned. His coat was damp at the shoulders, and his boots were dark with mud.

“By Caelan. By his solicitor, if necessary.”

“Then they are not mine to amend.”

Alric’s face tightened. “You know what he is offering. Harrowmere will take the mill if the debt is called. The Crown may revoke the timber license. Then the silver tract, the cottages, the stores—”

“I know.”

“And when the bailiffs come, they will sell the horses and put people in the road. You think Caelan cruel? Harrowmere’s men will be worse. They will have no reason to pretend otherwise.”

Elianor looked down at the articles. She saw the Dallow cottage as she had seen it from the hill: empty, its door crooked, rain entering through the broken roof. A house could be lost and still remain standing. That was the lesson of Greyfen.

“What happens if I refuse?” she asked.

Alric’s silence answered first.

“Your creditors move,” he said. “Caelan withdraws his settlement. I cannot hold everything together.”

“You have not held it together.”

“I have held it this long.”

“And what have you preserved?”

He glanced toward the corridor, where servants’ footsteps passed and faded.

“People.”

“Which people?”

He had no answer.

Elianor carried the articles to the hearth, then stopped before the dying fire. “If I marry him, the servants remain employed.”

“For as long as the articles bind him.”

“The tenants keep their leases.”

“For as long as they pay.”

“The stores will open when grain runs short.”

“He has not agreed to that.”

“Then he will.”

“Elianor.”

“He will,” she repeated, though she did not know whether she believed it. “I will make him agree.”

Her father gave a tired, bitter laugh. “You think you can make Lord Caelan Arbridge do anything?”

“No. But I can give him what he wants in exchange for what I need.”

“That is not a marriage. It is a negotiation.”

“It is the only kind available to me.”

He reached for her hand, but she stepped away.

“I will marry him,” she said.

The words settled between them.

Alric stared. “You are certain?”

“No.”

“Then do not say it.”

“I am certain that refusing will not save anyone. If Greyfen is taken, those who suffer first will not be you or me. Caelan has already begun governing this house. If I remain outside the bargain, he will make terms with everyone else without me.”

“You could go to your aunt in Eastmere.”

“And leave you here to sign everything alone?”

“I am your father.”

“You are afraid.”

His eyes closed briefly.

“Yes,” he said. “I am.”

For a moment she nearly embraced him. Then she remembered the Dallow children and the labor lists. Her father’s fear had not made him wicked. It had made him obedient to wickedness.

“I will do what I can from within the house,” she said.

That afternoon she went to the falconry by the covered passage. She wore a dark wool cloak and carried no maid. Rain blew beneath the eaves in cold needles.

Oren was absent. The goshawk’s old perch stood empty, its leather jesses coiled beneath it. A few pale feathers clung to the straw.

Elianor waited until the light faded.

When Tomas appeared, he came from the woods, soaked through. Mud stained his boots and climbed his trousers. He stopped when he saw her.

“You should not be here.”

“I know.”

“Does Caelan know?”

“No.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

He closed the door. Water dripped from his hair onto the packed earth.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That means something has.”

She almost smiled. “You have become difficult.”

“I was difficult before.”

“Yes. Before, you hid it better.”

His guardedness had sharpened since their argument in the gallery. It hurt her more than she let him see.

“I have something for you,” he said.

From beneath his coat he drew a waxed bundle and a folded paper sealed with dark gray wax. Elianor recognized Caelan’s seal.

She broke it.

The order was brief: search for agitators, seize grain as compensation, remove leaders before spring. Southmere and Fenwatch were among the villages named. At the bottom, in another hand, were the words:

*Greyfen servants—question separately. Begin with falconry.*

Elianor read it twice.

“Is it genuine?”

“I do not know.”

“But you believe it is.”

“I have seen what followed it.”

He told her of Southmere’s grain and boat being taken, of two sons carried away for road labor, of a discharged captain at Fenwatch beaten beside the river. Then he gave her the copied labor rolls: one set showing what tenants owed, another what they had paid.

“Why did you not tell me?”

“You asked me to leave.”

“I asked you to stop deciding what I was permitted to know.”

“I know.”

“And now you bring this because Mara told you to?”

His silence confirmed it.

“So you trust her with your life, and I receive what remains after she decides I am ready.”

“That is not fair.”

“No. It is not.”

He stepped toward her. “I kept you out of it because everyone who knows becomes someone Caelan can use. He is already questioning the falconry. He has threatened my father. If he finds these—”

“He will find them if we do nothing.”

“I know.”

“Then what are you asking me to do?”

“Choose.”

The word struck her.

“I have chosen,” she said. “I am going to marry Caelan.”

Tomas stared at her.

“No.”

“It has been decided.”

“By you?”

“By necessity.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is when one person’s choice holds a roof over hundreds of heads.”

“You think he will protect them because you ask prettily?”

“I think I can make him sign protections.”

“He will sign whatever keeps you quiet until the vows are spoken.”

“Then I will keep him from being quiet afterward.”

Tomas laughed once. “You still believe this is a table where both sides sit as equals.”

“No. I believe he wants something badly enough to listen.”

“He wants Greyfen.”

“He wants my name and the authority attached to it.”

“He wants you.”

“Not as you mean.”

“Does that comfort you?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because I can save lives.”

“By giving him yours.”

“Yes.”

The answer came too quickly. It frightened them both.

Tomas turned away, fists tightening at his sides. “You call it sacrifice. That makes it clean.”

“It is not clean.”

“It is noble. You can endure anything if you give it a noble name.”

She flinched. “You think I want this?”

“I think you want to believe you have no choice.”

“Perhaps I can choose to let the Dallow children sleep in a shed while we run into the marsh. Perhaps I can watch Caelan’s men take the stores, dismiss the servants, and sell the horses because I wanted freedom.”

“I never said we would abandon them.”

“What else would we do?”

“Open the gates. Take the records. Let people see what has been done.”

“And then?”

“Then they decide together.”

“People starving in the rain do not decide together. They fight over bread.”

“Sometimes fighting is the only language left.”

“And sometimes it kills the people who were already losing.”

His anger broke through his hurt. “You would rather trust Caelan than trust me.”

“I would rather trust what I can place in writing than what men promise in the dark.”

The words remained between them.

Tomas stepped back.

Elianor wanted to call him back. She wanted to tear the articles in half, throw Caelan’s order into the fire, and follow Tomas wherever he went. But she saw the empty cottage, the servants’ frightened faces, the road dissolving beneath the rain.

“I love you,” she said.

He closed his eyes.

“That is not enough.”

“No.”

“It should have been.”

“I know.”

He opened his eyes. The love in them was more terrible than anger. “If you marry him, he will use you to make his power appear merciful.”

“Then I will make him spend that mercy.”

“And when he stops pretending?”

“Then I will face it.”

“You already are.”

He turned toward the door.

“Tomas.”

He paused.

“Do not do anything reckless,” she said. “No blood. No heroic gesture. If Caelan dies, they will make a cause of his death and a gallows of everyone near him.”

“And if you marry him, they will make a crown of your surrender.”

“Perhaps. But I will be alive to break it.”

He looked back. For an instant she saw them beneath the trees, sharing a cloak while the wounded goshawk tested its wing. She felt again the warmth of his mouth against hers, the impossible belief that a life might be made rather than inherited.

Then the moment passed.

“I hope,” Tomas said quietly, “that your bargain is stronger than winter.”

He opened the door.

Elianor wanted to say that winter ended. She wanted to say this was not farewell, that love could survive what people did to it.

Instead she said, “Take care of Oren.”

Tomas’s mouth twisted.

“Take care of yourself,” he replied.

He stepped into the rain and disappeared beyond the covered passage.

Elianor remained in the mews, holding the marriage articles in one hand and Caelan’s sealed order in the other. The paper had dampened at the edges. Ink blurred beneath her thumb, spreading like a stain.

She thought of the bargain she had made.

She thought of the man she loved walking alone toward the woods.

Neither thought offered shelter.

chapters.name: The Last Hunting Season
chapters.content:
The snow came at last, mixed with rain. By morning, the courtyard was black mud crusted with ice, and the western road had vanished beneath drifts and standing water. No cart could reach Greyfen without breaking an axle.

Inside, wedding preparations continued.

The seamstresses had taken possession of the blue room. Elianor’s gown hung unfinished from a beam while Caelan’s steward circulated lists of guests, servants, horses, candles, and provisions. The lists grew longer as the stores grew shorter.

Elianor stood in the pantry doorway while Nella counted oat loaves into a basket.

“Two for the kitchens,” Elianor said. “Four to the infirmary. One to each of the north cottages.”

Nella hesitated. “My lady, the steward said no bread is to leave the manor without his mark.”

“Use mine.”

“He has men in the hall.”

“Let them see.”

Nella filled the basket. Before she could cover it, Caelan’s steward appeared. Venn was narrow-faced and perpetually disapproving.

“Lord Caelan has ordered the grain stores sealed until the creditor delegation arrives,” he said.

“The north families have no flour.”

“Their rents are in arrears.”

“They have paid in labor.”

“Labor does not fill a ledger.”

“It repaired the south bridge.”

“Which was an estate obligation.”

“Then the estate can feed the people who repaired it.”

Venn’s gaze fell to the basket. “Lord Caelan cannot permit sentimental distributions to undermine the accounts.”

Elianor looked at the bread. “Tell him I have assumed responsibility for the lives counted in those accounts.”

Venn bowed stiffly and withdrew.

“Should I put it back?” Nella asked.

“No.”

The bread went out through the laundry passage. By supper, Caelan had sent for Elianor.

He stood in the west hall beside a table covered with wedding plans. One hand rested on a column of figures.

“Your concern for the tenants is admirable,” he said.

“I am relieved to hear it.”

“It is also expensive.”

“A few loaves?”

“A precedent.” He lifted a paper. “You have requested that the Dallows’ eviction be delayed until spring.”

“I requested that they be allowed to return.”

“That cannot be done. Their labor arrears remain unpaid.”

“They repaired the south bridge. Their son is ill. Their cottage is empty.”

Caelan regarded her calmly. “You think an empty cottage proves the wisdom of mercy. I think it proves that mercy has already cost the estate a usable holding.”

“They were driven into a sheep shed.”

“Temporarily.”

“Return the cottage. Write off the arrears.”

“You are not yet mistress here.”

“Nor are you.”

“Not in name.”

The words settled between them.

“The western road must be repaired before the thaw,” he continued. “The Crown timber officer will not renew the license if the loads cannot pass. Harrowmere will call in its note. Kestrel Bank will seize the mill. The silver tract is already pledged. Do you understand what your generosity would purchase?”

“Bread.”

“At the price of the estate.”

“The estate is not preserved by starving everyone who works it.”

“Everything is preserved by choosing what can be lost.”

The great doors stood behind him, beside crates marked with Arbridge’s iron-gray seal. Even Greyfen’s furniture had begun to acquire destinations.

“You speak as if you already own this house,” she said.

“I speak as if I am the only person willing to keep it standing.”

Her father entered before she could answer. Alric looked exhausted, his hair silvered by the season.

“What is this?”

“Your daughter has authorized grain distributions and proposes forgiving arrears,” Caelan said.

“The Dallows need their cottage,” Elianor replied. “The north families need food.”

“And the road needs labor,” Alric said. “The Crown needs proof we can fulfill the timber contract. Harrowmere needs payment.”

“They need people alive enough to do those things.”

Alric flinched.

Caelan placed a hand on the table. “I have offered to settle the immediate obligations on the understanding that Greyfen will be administered according to my recommendations after the marriage.”

“After,” Elianor said.

“Every day before the marriage is a day in which the estate may fail.”

“Amend the articles. Guarantee the servants’ positions for a year. Release grain. Return the Dallows to their cottage.”

Caelan’s expression barely changed. “You ask for guarantees as though paper can bind necessity.”

“Paper binds debt.”

“Debt is enforced by power.”

“Then write the protections and let us see whose power is stronger.”

A flicker of amusement crossed his face. “You are learning.”

“I am learning that courtesy is a softer word for control.”

Alric looked between them. “Elianor.”

She folded her gloves. “I have said what I intend.”

Caelan gathered the papers. “I will consider your requests.”

By morning, the bread had been entered into the accounts as an advance against the six cottages, payable in labor at double rate. The Dallow eviction remained in place. Three other families had been marked for removal after the creditor gathering.

Elianor carried the account to her father.

“You signed this,” she said.

Alric looked at the seal. “Caelan had authority to use it.”

“You gave him that authority.”

“I gave him what was necessary.”

“No. You gave him what he asked for because you were afraid to refuse.”

His face tightened. “I have spent twenty years keeping this house from falling. Every time I chose one family over another, I chose the one whose loss would destroy the estate. Do you think I enjoyed it?”

“No.”

“Then do not look at me as if I am Caelan.”

“I look at you as the man who opens the door for him.”

Alric lowered his head, then returned to the road estimates.

That afternoon, in the stable yard, Tomas heard that the wedding would cost more lives than the feast.

He was carrying oats toward the falconry when voices drifted from the tack room. Bram, one of the younger stable hands, was speaking to old Hett.

“They counted the rooms again,” Bram said. “Venn had a list.”

“Of what?”

“Who stays and who goes.”

“After the marriage?”

“Soon after. Caelan wants his own men. Says Vey servants are too loyal to the old order.”

“And us?”

“Keep your head down and pray you’re useful.”

Tomas entered with the oats. Bram went pale.

“Who is on the list?” Tomas asked.

Bram glanced at Hett. “Kitchen girls. Two grooms. The laundry girl. Pask from the stores. Half the housemaids.”

“And falconry?”

Silence answered him.

Hett began brushing an already clean saddle. “Oren’s name was not on the copy I saw.”

“Mine?”

“Your name had a mark beside it,” Bram said. “Questioning.”

Tomas set down the sack. Caelan needed no proof, only an accusation. Oren was old, dependent, and easy to threaten. Tomas left before the others could read his face.

He found Mara at dusk beyond the old quarry. Snow gathered in her dark hair as she crouched beside a small, smokeless fire.

“They are making dismissal lists,” he told her.

“Then the wedding is closer than they claim.”

“The creditor gathering comes first.”

“Which is why we need a route through the marsh before the roads are watched entirely.”

She unrolled a scrap of cloth marked with charcoal lines. “From the forester’s lodge, follow the stream to the reed beds. The old causeway is passable only at low water. The western road is already watched.”

“The ridge?”

“Too exposed. The mill?”

“Watched.”

Tomas studied the map. “There is a drainage channel behind the abandoned limekiln.”

“Filled with ice.”

“Not all the way to the marsh.”

Mara folded the cloth. “If you leave, do not leave for romance. Leave because you understand what staying makes you.”

He thought of Elianor beneath Caelan’s hand, bargaining for protections that could not restrain the man who granted them.

“She will not come,” he said.

“You have not asked.”

“She has chosen the house.”

“She has chosen the people in it.”

“And Caelan will use that choice against her.”

“Yes.”

The answer’s simplicity unsettled him.

Tomas stared into the fire. “I do not know whether restraint is mercy or cowardice anymore.”

“Then decide before someone else decides for you.”

Night had fallen when Elianor left Greyfen.

She wore a plain brown cloak and carried no lantern. The snow had hardened across the paths, and each step cracked beneath her boots. She told herself she had come to warn Tomas about the questioning order. The truth was less orderly.

The forester’s lodge stood black among the trees. A light showed behind one shutter.

Tomas opened the door before she knocked.

For several breaths neither spoke.

“You should not be here,” he said.

“I know.”

“Caelan may have followed you.”

“He did not.”

“You cannot know that.”

“No,” she said. “I cannot.”

He shut the door. The lodge still held the remnants of their refuge: the low table, the cracked cup, the strip of linen once used to bind the goshawk’s wing. The perch near the hearth was empty.

“I heard about the lists,” she said.

His mouth hardened. “Did you hear your name?”

“My name is not on any list.”

“Because you are to be married.”

“Do not say it as though I made that choice lightly.”

“I did not say lightly.”

“Then how?”

He turned to the fire. “As though it were still a choice.”

She had no answer.

“Mara found a route through the marsh,” he said. “The soldiers watch the roads, not the reed channels. There is a drainage cut beyond the limekiln.”

“Why tell me?”

“Because you came.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is the only one I have.”

She moved closer. “You think I am a coward.”

“I think you are bargaining with men who have decided what you are worth.”

“And you think rebellion will save everyone?”

“I think it may give them a chance.”

“At what? Empty cottages? Retaliation? Gallows?”

His shoulders tightened. “You warned me not to become a hero.”

“I warned you not to die for the satisfaction of proving Caelan cruel.”

“And you will live beside him to prove you are merciful?”

She slapped him.

The sound was small beneath the storm.

Tomas did not move. His lack of defense undid her anger.

“I am afraid,” she whispered. “I am afraid that if I refuse him, the house falls before I can protect anyone. I am afraid that if I marry him, he will take every promise back after the vows. I am afraid I have mistaken endurance for courage.”

Tomas reached toward her, then stopped.

“I am afraid too,” he said.

“You hide it better.”

“No. I make it look like anger.”

She crossed the space between them. He held her carefully, as if she might break or vanish.

“I was cruel to you,” she said.

“You were right about some of it.”

“So were you.”

“I know.”

She tightened her arms around him. “That is not reconciliation.”

“No.”

“What is it?”

“A truce.”

“Until when?”

“Until one of us says something foolish.”

“You mean until I marry Caelan.”

His arms tightened.

“I do not know what to do,” she said.

“Neither do I.”

They sat beside the dying fire, holding hands while the storm struck the roof.

At last Tomas said, “If you need to find me, come by the old limekiln. Not the road. Follow the stream until the stones turn white.”

“Why would I need to find you?”

He did not answer.

She lifted his hand and kissed his knuckles. “I am still angry with you.”

“I am still angry with you.”

“Good.”

He looked toward the shutter, toward Greyfen hidden beyond the woods. “Good?”

“It means we have not become strangers.”

“No,” he said. “Not yet.”

Outside, somewhere in the dark, a hawk cried once. They listened until the sound faded, while the manor prepared for a wedding and the paths through the marsh waited beneath the ice.

chapters.name: Beyond the Marsh
chapters.content:
## Beyond the Marsh

By evening the snow had stopped, but the cold remained in the trees. It held the branches in a white, brittle grip and turned the path to the forester’s lodge into a narrow ribbon between drifts.

Elianor walked beneath the hood of her plain cloak, carrying a small lantern taken from the servants’ passage. She had left Greyfen by the laundry stair after Nella distracted the guard with a basin of linen. She had not told Nella where she was going. She had only said that she needed air, and Nella, understanding more than she asked, had looked away.

Behind her, the manor lamps shone gold through the trees. From a distance Greyfen looked peaceful: warm, prosperous, secure. No one seeing it would have guessed that its stores were sealed, its servants watched, and its lord’s seal had become another man’s instrument.

At the edge of the wood, Tomas stepped from the shadows.

He wore a dark coat over his work clothes, the collar turned against the cold. Snow silvered his hair. A leather satchel hung at his side.

“You came,” he said.

“You told me to.”

“I told you to find me if you needed me.”

“I did not know there was a difference.”

His mouth tightened, though not quite in anger. He took the lantern and led her toward the lodge.

Inside, the air smelled of ash and dried herbs. A fire burned low in the hearth. On the table stood a loaf of bread, cheese, two apples, and a stoppered flask. Beside them lay a blanket, a coil of rope, a tinderbox, and a narrow knife.

Elianor stared at the arrangement.

“No,” she said.

Tomas closed the door. “You do not know what I was going to say.”

“I know what those things mean.”

He set the lantern down. “Then say it.”

“You are leaving.”

“I am asking you to leave with me.”

The fire gave a soft crack.

“Tomorrow,” he continued. “Before dawn.”

She looked toward the shuttered window. “The wedding has not even been set.”

“Caelan does not need a wedding date to own the road, the stores, or your father’s seal.”

“He has not married me yet.”

“He has begun dismissing people as if he had.”

She turned away. The promises she had carried through every fitting and negotiation rose before her: a one-year guarantee for the servants, the release of grain, the return of the Dallows to their cottage. She had meant to trade Caelan the name and authority he wanted for protections he could not easily withdraw.

But he had already shown her what paper meant when the man holding power could tear it.

“And where would we go?” she asked.

“Through the marsh.”

“The old causeway is watched.”

“Not the causeway. The stream. The water still runs beneath the ice in places. Mara knows the crossings. Beyond the border there is a safehouse.”

“A rebel safehouse.”

“A house where no one will ask what we were born to.”

“They will ask what I have done.”

“They will ask what you are willing to do.”

The words struck sharply. He saw it and stepped toward her.

“Elianor—”

“No. You are right.”

He stopped.

“If I marry him, I become the hand that signs what he places before me. If I remain unmarried but under his authority, I am still the daughter of the house that invited him in. If I flee, I become a traitor and abandon everyone who cannot flee.”

“You are not abandoning them by refusing to help Caelan rule them.”

“And what happens when he takes Greyfen? He will punish more than me. He has already marked people for questioning. Your father’s name is on those lists.”

“Oren’s name is not.”

“Not yet.”

Tomas looked down. His silence confirmed what he would not say.

She moved closer to the fire. “If I go, he takes the estate without anyone inside who knows the records, the threatened tenants, the servants who have nowhere else to sleep.”

“If you stay, he will use you to make everything appear lawful.”

She flinched.

“I know what I am asking,” he said. “But if you remain, you will be made into his authority. He will put your name beside every eviction and every seizure.”

“And if I leave?”

“You may still help them. From somewhere he cannot reach.”

“You cannot promise that.”

“No.”

“Can you promise the rebels will not turn on Greyfen?”

“No.”

“Can you promise they will not see me as another noble who discovered justice only when her own walls began to shake?”

“No.” His gaze held hers. “I can promise to stand beside you when they say it.”

Her breath caught.

He reached for her hand. “I know you would rather be hated for failing everyone than loved for saving only yourself.”

“And you?”

“I would rather be poor with you than useful to the man who will hang me.”

The simplicity of it undid her. She laughed once, without humor, and wiped her eyes.

“That is not much of a life.”

“No.”

“There may be no bed.”

“Then we sleep on the floor.”

“I cannot cook.”

“I can.”

“You burn everything.”

“Only onions.”

“You have never mended a hem.”

“I have watched Oren mend a glove.”

“That is not the same.”

“It will be enough.”

She sat on the edge of the table. “What would I do?”

“Whatever you wanted.”

The answer frightened her more than any command.

“I do not know what that is.”

“Then we will find out.”

She imagined a life beyond Greyfen: no ancestral portraits, no receiving rooms, no one measuring her words for signs of disobedience. She might carry water, sort grain, learn the names of people who did not know hers. She might live in a house with a leaking roof and a garden choked by weeds. Tomas might come home with mud on his boots and an armful of wood. They might be poor, hungry, and free to be foolish together.

The vision was so modest it seemed impossible.

“And if we have children?” she asked.

His face softened.

“Then they will know they are not owned.”

“And if they are hungry?”

“Then we will be hungry with them.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only honest one I have.”

She reached for him. His hand closed around hers, rough and warm.

“I cannot promise to stop caring what happens to Greyfen,” she said.

“I would not ask it.”

“I cannot promise never to wish to return.”

“Neither can I.”

“I cannot promise I will forgive you for taking me away.”

“You may blame me all the way to the border.”

“And if I become frightened?”

“I will ask whether you are choosing or only obeying fear.”

She lowered her head against his chest.

For a while they stood that way, listening to the wind move through the pines. Then Tomas told her the route. They would follow the stream to the stones that turned white, crawl through the drainage channel behind the abandoned limekiln, and meet Mara beyond it. If the cart could not reach them, they would walk. The border might take two days, perhaps three.

“You have thought of this for some time,” Elianor said.

“I have thought of it every time I looked at you and wondered how long we had left.”

“Why did you not ask before?”

“Because I knew you would say no.”

“I might have said yes.”

“You might have believed you had to.”

“And now?”

“Now I am asking you to choose.”

The word had become a wound between them, used too often and never trusted. Yet he was not asking her to choose him over the tenants. He was asking whether she would remain where every road ended in Caelan’s hand.

She leaned up and kissed him.

It began almost as an apology. Then his hand rose to the back of her neck, and the cold, the snow, and the laws that separated them fell away. He kissed her as if they had been denied time and had decided to spend what remained without measuring it.

They ate beside the fire, sharing bread and cheese. Tomas explained which boots would hold on marsh ice and which paths avoided the watchmen. Elianor told him about the blue room and the seamstresses, about one woman sewing pearls into a sleeve while the cook counted lentils for supper.

“Perhaps that is what I will do beyond the border,” she said. “Count lentils.”

“You will be very important.”

“More important than you?”

“Certainly. I burn onions.”

He smiled, and the sight of it hurt her.

Later he found warmed wine beneath the hearthstone. They passed the cup between them.

“What will you call me?” she asked.

“When?”

“When we cross the border. If someone asks.”

“Your name.”

“That will be dangerous.”

“Then we will give them another.”

“What?”

He studied her. “Nell.”

She frowned. “That is a kitchen girl’s name.”

“Then it will suit you.”

“And you?”

“Tom.”

“That is worse.”

“It is practical.”

“It is ugly.”

“You may call me something better.”

“Thomas Vale, who burns onions.”

“That is too long for a border crossing.”

She laughed, and the sound made the little room seem larger.

They slept on the narrow bed with their clothes on, the blanket drawn over them. Elianor lay with her back against Tomas’s chest, his arm around her waist. Near midnight she turned to face him.

“I am afraid,” she whispered.

“So am I.”

“I have never been this afraid.”

“I have.”

“When?”

“When you struck me.”

“You deserved it.”

“I did.”

“And when I said I would marry Caelan?”

“You deserved that.”

“I did not.”

“No.” His fingers touched her sleeve. “You deserved a choice that did not hurt anyone.”

“There may be no such choice.”

“I know.”

She touched his cheek. “If we go and it is terrible—”

“It will be terrible.”

“Do not interrupt me.”

“I am sorry.”

“If we quarrel, you must not leave without telling me.”

“I promise.”

“If I ask to turn back?”

“I will ask whether you are choosing or only obeying fear.”

She closed her eyes.

“Do you still think I chose privilege over you?”

“No.”

“Do you still think you are a coward?”

His expression tightened. “I do not know.”

“Then do not decide tonight.”

He kissed her brow. “Tonight I am only yours.”

The words could not be witnessed or enforced. They belonged to the dark, the small lodge, and the hours before their lives divided. Elianor held him and let herself believe them.

She slept.

When she woke, the fire had become embers and Tomas stood beside the table fastening the satchel.

For one terrible instant she thought he had left without her.

“I was not leaving,” he said.

“You were standing.”

“I can see how that resembles betrayal.”

She threw the blanket at him. He caught it, smiling.

“An hour before dawn,” he said.

“Give me ten minutes.”

“I have given you all the time I can.”

She dressed quickly. Tomas tied the provisions beneath her cloak and checked the knife at her belt. His fingers lingered there.

“You may have to use it.”

“On whom?”

“Anyone who tries to take you back.”

“And if it is Caelan?”

“Then do not hesitate.”

She placed her hand over his. “I am coming with you. I am not walking into a battle.”

“Neither am I.”

He opened the door.

Cold rushed inside. The forest waited, pale and indistinct. Behind them Greyfen was hidden by the trees, though its presence seemed to fill the whole world.

Elianor stepped over the threshold. Tomas followed and closed the door against the warmth.

They did not see the figure watching from the ridge above the eastern path, or the dark horse among the firs. They did not know that Caelan’s steward had spent the night questioning servants, offering some money, others dismissal, and one the safety of a sick child.

They knew only the snow, the narrow stream, and the whitened stones somewhere beyond the trees.

Hand in hand, they began walking toward the marsh.

chapters.name: The Betrayal
chapters.content:
## The Betrayal

The last stars had faded when Elianor and Tomas reached the stream.

Snow crusted the banks, but beneath it the water moved blackly toward the marsh. Tomas went first, testing each stone. Elianor followed in a brown wool skirt and cloak borrowed from Nella, wearing a man’s boots and a linen cap over her braided hair. She carried no jewels, no ring, nothing to mark her as Lady Elianor Vey.

Still, she had felt Greyfen watching her when she left through the laundry passage. The guard had turned away at the exact moment she passed. A kitchen girl had dropped her eyes. Somewhere behind the walls, a door had closed softly.

She had told herself that fear made signs where none existed.

Now she was not sure.

“Here,” Tomas whispered.

He reached for her hand as they crossed. His palm was cold.

“Two more crossings,” he said. “Then the white stones. The drainage channel is behind the limekiln. Mara will meet us beyond it.”

“I remember.”

“You have been awake all night.”

“So have you.”

For a moment they stood shoulder to shoulder beneath the bare trees. There was no manor, no wedding, no Caelan—only the dark woods and the road they had chosen.

Then a twig broke behind them.

They turned. Nothing moved among the trees.

Tomas’s hand went to the knife at his belt. Elianor heard only the stream, the wind, and her own breathing.

“Fox,” she whispered.

“Perhaps.”

He did not sound convinced.

They continued down toward the marsh. Tomas moved with the wary silence of one born to woods and weather. Elianor stumbled once, and he caught her before she fell.

“If we reach the safehouse,” she said, “what happens?”

“We sleep, if Mara permits it. Then we cross the border.”

His answer frightened her with its simplicity. Beyond the border lay no title, servants, or walls. There would be hunger and work, suspicion and uncertainty. She had thought she wanted that freedom, but behind her were Nella, Sella, Perran, Pask, Oren, the Dallows, and every tenant whose debt had been turned into a chain.

Fleeing would not erase their obligations. It would only remove her from the rooms where they were enforced.

Tomas sensed her hesitation. “You can still turn back.”

She looked sharply at him.

“I did not mean—”

“You promised not to disappear when we quarrel.”

“I promised to tell you if I wanted to turn back.”

“Do you?”

“No.” She took his hand again. “Wanting is not the same as doing.”

His fingers tightened around hers.

They were nearly at the old limekiln when Tomas stopped.

The ruins rose from the snow like the ribs of some dead animal. Behind them, under thorn and ash, was the drainage channel: a low opening beneath a collapsed wall, narrow enough to crawl through.

Tomas set down the pack and began pulling away the frozen weeds.

Then came the faint clink of metal.

A horse snorted somewhere among the trees.

Tomas shoved the pack into the channel. “Inside.”

“What?”

“Now.”

Elianor dropped to her knees. Tomas pushed her toward the opening. She crawled over sharp stones, clutching the pack before her. Behind her, he kicked snow over their tracks and followed, drawing the weeds across the entrance.

Darkness closed around them.

“Soldiers,” Elianor whispered.

“Not yet.”

Boots crushed the snow above. A man cursed at the cold. Another voice said, “Search the kiln.”

Tomas leaned near her ear. “There is another opening twenty paces through. It comes out beneath the ash bank.”

He began to crawl. Elianor followed, holding the pack against her chest. The passage narrowed, then widened. At its end, gray light filtered through roots.

Tomas stopped.

A shadow crossed the light.

He pulled her back against him.

Outside, a voice said, “They are here.”

The words were quiet and certain.

Tomas shoved the pack toward her. “When I go out, run left. The reeds will hide you.”

“To where?”

“Downhill.”

“You said there was no path.”

“There is enough of one.”

He turned to her. “They want me more than they want you. You are a lady. They will not harm you.”

“They have already harmed me.”

His face tightened. “Then let me give them what they came for.”

The soldiers had found the upper entrance. Stones shifted above them.

“I will not leave you,” Elianor said.

“You may have to.”

The first soldier broke through. Light flooded the passage. Tomas raised both hands.

“I am Tomas Vale,” he called. “The lady is unharmed. Take me to your commander and let her go.”

A laugh answered him.

“Lord Caelan will decide what happens to both of you.”

Tomas looked back once. “When I move, run.”

He struck the first soldier as the man crawled into the channel, driving him against the wall. A second soldier seized Tomas by the collar. Tomas kicked and twisted, but more men forced their way through.

Elianor tried to pass them. Someone caught her braid and pulled her backward. She slashed with the knife, cutting cloth, but a blow to her wrist sent the weapon into the darkness.

“Tomas!”

He drove an elbow into a soldier’s face and almost broke free. A cudgel struck the side of his head.

He sagged.

Elianor clawed at the earth, caught his boot, and was dragged from the channel by two men. Snow struck her face. Around the kiln stood eight soldiers in dark cloaks, their horses steaming in the cold.

Tomas knelt among them, blood darkening his hair.

“Do not touch her,” he said.

A mounted man approached from the trees. Elianor recognized Caelan’s steward. He dismounted and studied her plain clothes, then the open pack in the snow.

Bread. Cheese. Apples. Rope. A blanket.

The small, domestic evidence of the life they had meant to begin.

“Lady Elianor,” he said. “You have caused considerable alarm.”

“Where is Lord Caelan?”

“On his way.”

Tomas tried to stand. A soldier struck him across the shoulders and forced him down.

Elianor struggled against the hands holding her. “Release him!”

The steward lifted the flask from the pack and examined it. “Did you truly think to reach the border on foot?”

“I thought to reach somewhere beyond your authority.”

“That is precisely the difficulty.”

Tomas spat blood into the snow. “Tell Caelan to come himself if he wants to parade his courage.”

The steward’s expression did not change. “He will.”

Elianor looked at Tomas. His wrists were being bound behind him. Blood ran from his temple, bright against his pale face.

“I am sorry,” she whispered.

“Do not be.”

“I brought you into this.”

“You came because you chose.”

“They will use it against you.”

“They were using everything against us already.”

The steward stepped between them. “Enough.”

He nodded to the soldiers. Tomas was hauled upright. Elianor was dragged toward the horses. She kicked free once, but a guard caught her shoulders. Her borrowed cloak tore, revealing the gray wool beneath. At the cuff was the Vey stitching.

“So she is a lady after all,” the guard muttered.

Elianor struck him across the mouth.

His hand rose.

“Touch her,” Tomas said, “and I will make you swallow your own teeth when these ropes come off.”

The guard paused. Another soldier brought the cudgel down.

Tomas folded into the snow.

Elianor screamed and lunged toward him, but the men held her fast. The steward caught her chin and turned her face toward him.

“Control yourself, my lady.”

“Do not call me that.”

“Whether you accept the title or not, it is why you will be treated better than he is.”

The words were worse than a threat.

Behind them, riders emerged through the trees. At their center came Caelan on a gray horse, his dark coat untouched by the weather. He dismounted and handed the reins to a soldier.

He looked first at Elianor’s loosened hair and torn cloak, then at Tomas.

For the first time since she had known him, Caelan smiled without courtesy.

“Now we know what all those absences meant.”

“You knew.”

“I suspected. Suspicion is a poor instrument. Evidence is more useful.”

He glanced at the pack.

“You have provided me with enough.”

Tomas stirred. “Go to hell.”

Caelan regarded him briefly. “Take him separately. Bring Lady Elianor back to Greyfen.”

“No,” she said.

Caelan turned to her. “You will not take me anywhere.”

“I have already taken Greyfen,” he replied. “The accounts, the seal, the servants, the roads, the grain. All that remained was your cooperation.”

“I will never give it.”

“You need not.” He stepped closer. “After today, no one will believe you left innocently. Your father cannot defend you without destroying himself. The household cannot conceal you without being accused of aiding an abduction. The servants will answer questions. Every one of them.”

Elianor imagined Sella’s fevered face, Nella’s lowered eyes, Pask in the stores, Oren in the falconry yard. Caelan had not merely captured two fugitives. He had been handed a key to every locked room in Greyfen.

“You threatened them,” she said.

“I offered them choices.”

“You offered someone the safety of a sick child.”

A flicker crossed the steward’s face.

Elianor saw it. Caelan saw that she saw it. His expression became thoughtful.

“Who betrayed us?” she demanded.

No one answered. The soldiers stared at the snow. The steward looked away.

Tomas was dragged toward a horse. “Elianor,” he called.

She strained toward him. “I’m here.”

“Do not let them make you ashamed.”

Caelan’s hand closed around her arm.

She looked once at the path behind them: the stream, the firs, the hidden lodge where they had imagined a life no one could own. Snow was already filling their footprints.

“Tomas,” she said.

His mouth moved in answer.

Then the horses carried them toward Greyfen. Tomas was forced onto one mount, his bound hands tied to the saddle before him. Elianor was lifted onto another and placed between two guards.

Behind them, the limekiln sank into the snow, holding the last dark traces of their escape.

chapters.name: A Public Shame
chapters.content:
By noon, the rain had turned the courtyard to black mud.

It fell in a fine, unceasing veil, silvering the iron chains around the well and running from the mouths of the stone gargoyles above the gate. Servants had been driven from the kitchens, stables, laundry, and storehouse to stand beneath the covered walkways. Tenant families were gathered beyond them, their wet cloaks dark against the walls. Soldiers lined the courtyard in two ranks, their spears upright, their faces expressionless.

At the center stood a wooden platform.

Elianor saw it from the upper gallery before the guards came for her.

They had dressed her in the blue wool gown she had worn when Caelan first visited Greyfen. Her hair had been combed and braided despite the dried blood at her temple. Someone had washed the mud from her boots and replaced them with soft slippers. Her bruised wrist was wrapped in clean linen. The care was not kindness. It was preparation.

A lady must look like a lady when she was disgraced.

Caelan waited at the end of the gallery, immaculate in a black riding coat untouched by rain. His gray eyes moved over her face, lingering on the bandage, the loose strand of hair near her cheek, the hand she held close to her ribs.

“You will come quietly,” he said.

Elianor looked past him toward the courtyard. “Where is Tomas?”

“Being brought before the household.”

“Is he alive?”

Caelan’s expression did not alter. “You should be concerned with whether you are.”

She turned to him then. “If you have killed him—”

“You will not improve his condition by making a scene.”

The guards stepped closer. Elianor could feel their expectation: that she would plead, perhaps collapse, perhaps remember the rules of her birth and behave as someone worth protecting. Caelan had returned her to Greyfen not as a daughter but as evidence. He meant to display the proof of her disobedience until even those who pitied her were afraid to say so.

“Why a hearing?” she asked.

“Because the household deserves to know what happened.”

“No. Because you want them to know what you say happened.”

A faint smile touched his mouth. “The distinction will not matter by evening.”

He offered his arm.

She did not take it. The guards flanked her instead, and together they descended the stairs.

The courtyard smelled of wet straw, horse sweat, and woodsmoke struggling in the damp. A murmur passed through the servants as Elianor emerged. Nella stood near the laundry passage, pale and rigid beneath a gray shawl. Perran was beside her, his hands clenched at his sides. Oren had been forced forward with the falconers. His face seemed to have aged ten years since morning.

Elianor searched the crowd for Sella and found her near the kitchen door, one hand braced against the wall, the other pressed to her stomach. A guard stood behind her.

Then Tomas was brought out.

For one terrible instant Elianor did not recognize him. His face was swollen on one side, the cut at his temple crusted dark beneath his hair. His hands were bound behind him, and a rope ran from his wrists to the saddle of a soldier’s horse. He walked because the horse pulled him forward whenever he faltered.

His gaze found hers.

The courtyard disappeared around them.

He tried to straighten. It cost him visibly. His mouth moved, but no sound reached her through the rain.

“Elianor,” he said at last.

The guard holding the rope struck him between the shoulders with the butt of his spear.

She stepped forward. “Do not touch him.”

Tomas staggered but remained standing.

Caelan raised one gloved hand, and the soldiers closed around him. “You see,” he said to the assembled household, “how even now the accused attempts to influence Lady Elianor through intimidation.”

A few heads lowered. Others remained fixed on Tomas.

Caelan climbed the platform. A clerk followed with a bundle of papers and a small wooden box bearing the Vey seal. Lord Alric came last.

He wore no coat despite the rain. His gray hair was plastered to his forehead, and his shoulders had sunk beneath the weight of the seal Caelan carried for him. He looked toward Elianor only once.

She saw the answer there before he spoke: fear.

Not fear for Tomas. Not even fear for her.

Fear of the creditors, the Crown office, the estate being stripped from him stone by stone until nothing remained of the name Vey but a line in a ledger.

Caelan turned to the courtyard. “This man, Tomas Vale, son of Oren Vale, entered the forest lodge belonging to Greyfen without permission. He concealed himself there with Lady Elianor Vey. He supplied her with clothing and provisions and attempted to remove her from the estate by force.”

A sharp sound came from the crowd. Nella’s hand flew to her mouth.

“He did not remove me by force,” Elianor said.

Caelan looked at her. “You will speak when called upon.”

“I left willingly.”

The clerk began to read from the papers. “At approximately the fourth hour before dawn, the accused was found in possession of a knife, rope, tinder, food, and—”

“Those were mine,” Elianor said.

Caelan’s voice cut across hers. “—with the stated intention of crossing the western marsh and fleeing the jurisdiction of Lord Alric Vey.”

Tomas gave a broken laugh.

The soldier nearest him struck him again, this time in the ribs. Tomas folded, breathless.

Elianor lunged forward, but two guards seized her arms. Pain flashed through her bandaged wrist.

“Stop!” she cried.

The word rang against the stone.

Caelan waited until the courtyard had gone silent. “You may all observe Lady Elianor’s distress. It is precisely why this hearing is necessary. A young woman, deceived by a servant, has been placed in danger of abduction, dishonor, and permanent ruin.”

Tomas forced himself upright. Blood ran from the corner of his mouth.

“Look at me,” he said to Elianor.

She did.

“Do not let him make you ashamed.”

Caelan’s face hardened for the first time.

He descended from the platform and approached Tomas. “You presume much for a man who has been fed, housed, and employed at my future wife’s family’s expense.”

Tomas spat blood into the mud. “You mean a man you owned.”

A stir moved through the servants.

Caelan’s eyes swept over them. “This is what disobedience becomes when it is mistaken for courage.”

He seized Tomas by the jaw and turned his face toward the crowd. “He claims affection. Yet he led Lady Elianor into the woods in the dark, dressed her in a servant’s clothes, and prepared to take her beyond Greyfen’s protection. Had the patrol not found them, she might now be dead in the marsh—or in the hands of men less scrupulous than I.”

“You sent the patrol,” Elianor said.

“Yes. To protect you.”

“You knew where we were going.”

“I suspected.”

“You followed us.”

“I exercised my right to secure what belongs to Greyfen.”

The words settled over the courtyard more heavily than the rain.

What belongs to Greyfen.

Not what belonged to her. Not whom she loved. Not even whether she had chosen. Property, secured by force and justified by fear.

Alric flinched.

Elianor turned toward him. “Father.”

He would not meet her eyes.

“Tell them,” she said. “Tell them I went of my own will.”

Caelan did not stop her. That was the cruelty of it. He knew Alric would understand the trap.

Alric’s mouth opened. Rain ran down his face. “Elianor, you should not have left.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“The estate is in a dangerous position. Caelan has acted within his rights to prevent—”

“Within his rights?” Her voice shook, but she raised it. “He took your seal. He commands your guards. He searches your servants. He has seized grain and called it debt. Is that within your rights too?”

A soldier shifted uneasily.

Caelan’s clerk lowered his papers.

Alric looked at the gathered people—at Oren, at Nella, at the tenants crowded under the dripping eaves—and something like shame crossed his face. It vanished beneath exhaustion.

“I cannot discuss these matters here.”

“You cannot discuss them anywhere.”

“Enough,” Caelan said.

“No.” Elianor twisted against the guards. “You brought me here to make me a warning. Then let them hear the truth. I chose to leave. Tomas did not abduct me. He did not threaten me. He did not trick me. I went because I would rather live in a marsh with him than become the hand that signs away every cottage in Valedorn.”

A woman near the kitchen began to weep.

Caelan’s gaze moved to her. The weeping stopped.

“Elianor,” Alric said quietly, “you are making this worse.”

“For whom?”

“For everyone.”

Tomas looked at him with an expression more sorrowful than angry. “That is what they always say before they tighten the rope.”

Caelan nodded toward the soldiers.

They dragged Tomas to the foot of the platform and forced him to his knees. Oren made a sound low in his throat and stepped forward.

“Stay back,” a guard warned.

“He is my son.”

“And you are still employed at Lord Arbridge’s discretion.”

The threat struck Oren harder than any blow. He stopped.

Elianor understood then that Caelan had arranged every witness, every silence, every helpless face. He had not merely captured them in the woods. He had brought the whole estate into the snare. If she resisted, Tomas would suffer. If she pleaded, the servants would be questioned. If Alric defended her, Greyfen would be seized at once.

Caelan returned to the platform.

“By the authority entrusted to me by Lord Alric Vey,” he announced, lifting the seal, “Tomas Vale is found guilty of trespass upon noble property, conspiracy to abduct a lady of the house, unlawful possession of a weapon, and attempted flight from lawful custody.”

“That is a lie,” Elianor said.

“It is a judgment.”

“You have not permitted a defense.”

“The accused has spoken.”

Tomas looked up at him. “You call beating a man a hearing?”

The guard struck him across the face.

This time Oren broke through the line.

Three soldiers seized him before he reached the platform. One drove a fist into his stomach. He crumpled in the mud.

“Father!” Tomas shouted.

Caelan let the moment continue until Oren lay still.

Then he said, “The sentence is death by hanging, to be carried out at dawn tomorrow.”

A cry rose from the servants.

Elianor felt the world tilt beneath her. Her knees buckled, but the guards held her upright.

“No,” she whispered.

Caelan glanced at her. “The sentence may be reviewed after your marriage.”

Tomas turned toward her despite the soldiers restraining him. “Do not.”

Caelan smiled.

“He will remain alive,” he said, “provided you cease this childish defiance. You will return to your rooms. You will not speak with servants without permission. You will not leave the house. The wedding will proceed in three days, and afterward Lord Arbridge will determine what is to be done with the prisoner.”

“You mean you will hang him if I refuse.”

“I mean that your choices have consequences.”

Tomas strained against the ropes. “Elianor, listen to me. Do not marry him for me.”

A soldier struck him in the back of the head.

He fell sideways into the mud.

She screamed his name.

Caelan came close enough that only she could hear him. “You wanted freedom. Look carefully at its cost.”

Elianor stared at Tomas’s motionless body, at Oren kneeling beside him with a guard’s spear across his shoulders, at Nella crying silently near the laundry door.

Then she looked at Caelan.

For weeks she had tried to bargain with men who believed themselves reasonable. She had offered obedience for grain, marriage for protection, silence for the safety of servants. Each compromise had given Caelan another key, another signature, another piece of Greyfen to place beneath his hand.

She had thought herself clever enough to preserve something by surrendering something else.

There was nothing left to surrender that would satisfy him.

“You have already taken everything,” she said.

His expression remained calm. “Not everything.”

He gestured toward the guards.

They pulled Elianor away from the courtyard and up the stairs. She did not resist. Resistance here would only give him another spectacle. Behind her, Tomas was dragged toward the stables, his boots carving two dark trails through the mud.

At the top of the stairs, she looked back once.

The courtyard had begun to empty. Servants moved like shadows. Rain streamed from the roof. Oren remained on his knees beside the blood-darkened mud, while Caelan stood above him with the Vey seal in his hand.

A door closed between Elianor and the yard.

The guards took her to the west rooms, where the windows overlooked the chapel and the gallows being raised beneath the rain. A fire burned in the grate, but the room was cold. Her wet dress clung to her skin. One of the guards removed the latch from the inside door and replaced it with a bar on the outer side.

“Until the wedding,” he said.

Elianor faced the window.

Below, men were carrying beams across the courtyard.

The guard hesitated. “My lady—”

“Go.”

He shut the door.

She stood alone in the room Caelan had chosen for her, with her bruised wrist in her lap and Tomas’s blood still beneath her fingernails. Beyond the glass, the gallows took shape piece by piece.

She had believed that surrender might buy time.

Now she understood that time was another thing Caelan owned.

chapters.name: The Locked Room
chapters.content:
The key turned in the lock before the footsteps had faded.

Elianor stood with one hand against the door, listening to the guards settle beyond it. One leaned against the wall, judging by the scrape of leather and the soft knock of a shoulder against plaster. The other shifted his weight every few breaths. They had been instructed to watch her, not merely bar her in. Caelan trusted doors only when men stood behind them.

The room smelled of damp wool and rain. Water crawled down the windowpanes in silver threads, blurring the chapel beyond. Workers had raised the gallows in the courtyard beneath the western wall. Even from here she could see the dark crossbeam, the rope hanging from it like a line drawn through the air.

Tomas would be taken there at dawn.

She had tried not to think the words. They had remained words while Caelan spoke them in the courtyard, polished and bloodless beneath the rain. Now they had become a shape outside her window.

A servant had left a fire burning, but it was nearly dead. Elianor knelt and pushed at the logs with the iron poker. Ash spilled across the hearthstone. The movement pulled at her bruised wrist, and pain climbed her arm in a bright, narrow stroke.

She welcomed it. Pain was immediate. It did not ask her to imagine a rope.

On the table stood a tray she had not touched: broth filmed with grease, coarse bread, a cup of watered wine. Caelan would know whether she ate. Perhaps he had ordered the kitchen to report every mouthful, as though hunger and obedience could be measured in the same ledger.

She took the bread and broke it in half.

The first piece went into the dying fire.

The second she held until it warmed in her hand.

She thought of all the choices that had carried her here. They had not looked like choices when she made them. They had worn the faces of frightened tenants, empty granaries, her father’s shaking fingers over debt ledgers. They had arrived as small permissions.

Sign this.

Delay that eviction.

Trust me with the seal.

Marry me, and the servants will keep their places.

She had believed that yielding one inch might prevent a greater loss. Caelan had treated every inch as a road.

Beyond the window, a horse screamed.

Elianor crossed the room and pressed her forehead to the cold glass. The sound came again, shorter this time, followed by shouting from the stable yard. She could not see the stables from this angle, only the roofline and the tops of two ash trees stripped bare by winter.

Oren, she thought.

Or Tomas.

She closed her eyes.

The memory of the courtyard returned with cruel precision: Tomas on his knees, blood drying at his temple, the rope cutting into his wrists. His face had been pale beneath the rain, but his eyes had found hers. Not pleading. Never pleading. He had looked at her as if he could still reach her across the guards, the watching tenants, the whole machinery of Greyfen.

Do not let him make you ashamed.

She had not been ashamed of loving him. She was ashamed of how long she had mistaken surrender for protection.

A murmur passed in the corridor.

Elianor turned.

The guard outside said something too low to understand. A woman answered. There was a soft scuffle, then the sound of a basin being set down.

“Lady Elianor?” called Nella.

The guard muttered, “Leave it.”

“It’s linen for her wrist.”

“She has linen.”

“She has bled through that.”

A pause.

“Put it down and go.”

Nella’s steps retreated. Elianor waited until they had gone several paces, then said, “Nella.”

The footsteps stopped.

“Lady?”

“Come back.”

The guard cursed under his breath. Nella returned, and a moment later the lock opened. The nearer guard stood in the doorway, one hand on his sword. Nella entered carrying a basin and a folded cloth. Her face was lowered, but not before Elianor saw the fear in it.

“Set it there,” the guard ordered.

Nella obeyed. As she straightened, her fingers brushed the underside of the basin.

Something clicked against the wood.

The guard closed the door before Elianor could look.

For several breaths neither woman moved.

Then Elianor lifted the basin. Beneath it lay a small wooden button, the sort used on stable coats. A dark mark had been scratched across its face.

“Tomas?” she whispered.

Nella’s eyes filled, but she shook her head. “No. It’s a message.”

“From whom?”

“I don’t know. Perran gave it to me. He said Oren is alive.”

Elianor gripped the basin’s rim. “And Tomas?”

Nella swallowed. “They took him to the old tack room. The men say Caelan wants him kept there until morning.”

Alive, then. The word came with relief so violent it made her dizzy.

“Is he conscious?”

“I don’t know. Oren tried to follow. They struck him down.” Nella glanced at the door. “You mustn’t ask more.”

“Why not?”

“Because the walls have ears, and the ears have children.”

The sentence seemed to leave a bruise in the air.

Elianor looked at the barred door. “What does the mark mean?”

“It means the women are watching.”

“Watching what?”

“Who enters. Who leaves. Which guard drinks. Which one prays. Which one is afraid.” Nella’s voice trembled, but she kept speaking. “Mara used to say a house is never held by the lord who names it. It’s held by the hands that lift its doors.”

“Mara,” Elianor said. “Has she reached Greyfen?”

“No one knows.”

“Then how—”

“Nella!” the guard shouted from outside.

Nella flinched. She took up the basin.

“Wait,” Elianor said. “Tell them I need to see my father.”

The girl stared at her.

“Tell them I am ill if you must. Tell them I am dying. But bring him.”

Nella’s mouth tightened. “He may not come.”

“He will come.”

It was not confidence. It was the last remnant of being his daughter.

Nella opened the door. Before stepping through, she turned the wooden button in her palm and placed it on the mantel.

The guard saw nothing.

An hour passed. Or perhaps two. The rain thickened until the courtyard disappeared entirely. Elianor sat at the writing desk, though no paper had been given to her. She dipped a dry quill into the empty inkwell and dragged its point across the page, leaving pale scratches like the beginning of a confession.

At last, the key turned again.

Lord Alric entered alone.

He looked smaller than he had that morning. His coat hung loose at the shoulders, and his beard had gone gray at the edges in the space of a single day. The seal ring remained on his finger. Elianor stared at it until he noticed.

“You asked for me,” he said.

“I asked for my father.”

His face tightened. “I am your father.”

“No. You are the man who stood beside Caelan while he sentenced Tomas.”

Alric shut the door behind him. “Lower your voice.”

“There are guards outside.”

“That is why.”

“So they can hear what you have done?”

He crossed to the hearth but did not warm his hands. “You are distressed.”

“Tomas is to hang at dawn.”

“He was convicted under—”

“He was convicted because Caelan wanted a rope around my throat.”

Alric looked toward the window. “You should never have fled.”

“I should never have remained.”

“You would have been safe.”

“Safe?” She laughed, and the sound was so sharp that he winced. “You call this safe? He has locked me in my own rooms. He has taken your seal. He commands the servants, the stores, the courts, the guards. He publicly named me a liar because I told the truth.”

“I could not contradict him before the tenants.”

“You could have said that I left willingly.”

“You had been misled.”

“I had been awake.”

Alric’s hands closed at his sides. “You do not understand what is at stake.”

“I understand precisely. Greyfen is in debt. The mill is pledged. The silver tract is pledged. The timber rights are pledged. Three cottages are to be taken for bread that I ordered sent to sick people. The Dallows sleep outside a house they repaired. Caelan means to gather creditors here and turn every remaining stone into his property.”

“He means to settle the debts.”

“He means to own us.”

“He will keep the estate alive.”

“Alive for whom?”

Alric’s gaze snapped back to her. “For all of them. The servants. The tenants. The families you claim to defend. If Arbridge calls in the notes, Greyfen is finished. The Crown will seize the timber. Harrowmere will take the mill. Kestrel will take the land. You speak of cruelty as though there is a clean road through this.”

“There may not be a clean road. But there is a difference between being crushed and kneeling to the man holding the stone.”

He turned away.

Elianor saw the motion and understood that he had rehearsed his answers, but not for this question. “How long?” she asked.

“How long what?”

“How long have you known that he would take control?”

Alric said nothing.

“How long, Father?”

“Since autumn.”

The answer was barely audible.

She stepped back as if he had struck her. “Since autumn.”

“I was trying to prevent it.”

“By giving him the seal?”

“Temporarily.”

“By letting him alter the labor rolls?”

“To satisfy the creditors.”

“By letting him seize grain?”

“Against future labor.”

“By promising him my marriage?”

Alric’s face collapsed. For a moment he was only an old man in a cold room, frightened of the dark.

“I promised nothing without your consent.”

“You placed the promise in every room of this house. You made refusal impossible and called it consent when I stopped speaking.”

“I thought I could preserve your name.”

“My name?”

“House Vey has stood for four hundred years.”

“And what is it now?”

His eyes shone. “The last thing I can give you.”

“No,” she said. “It is the first thing you gave away.”

The rain beat against the glass.

Alric sank into the chair beside the hearth. “I have watched men lose everything for pride. Lands, children, lives. I thought if I bent, only the house would bend. I thought I could yield authority piece by piece and keep enough to protect you.”

“You surrendered authority piece by piece because you feared losing the family name.”

“Yes.”

The admission came without defense.

Elianor felt anger rise, but beneath it lay grief. “And now?”

“Now I have neither.”

“You still have a choice.”

His laugh was quiet and broken. “Do I?”

“You can withdraw your authority from Caelan. You can declare that the sentence was unlawful. You can order the guards to release Tomas.”

“And then?”

“Then we face what comes.”

“What comes is seizure. Soldiers. A trial in the capital, if we are fortunate. If we are not, Caelan’s men burn the villages that supported your escape. They hang Oren. They take Nella’s sister. They empty every store before spring.”

“He already means to do those things.”

Alric looked at her.

She held his gaze. “You know he does.”

For several seconds, only the rain spoke.

“I cannot save everyone,” he said.

“No. But you can stop helping him choose who suffers first.”

His head bowed.

A knock came at the door. Neither of them answered. Another followed, three quick taps, then one.

Alric looked up. “Who is that?”

Elianor went to the door. “Who?”

A man’s voice said, “Wood for the fire.”

“There is enough wood,” Alric said.

“Not by morning, my lord.”

The guard outside shifted. “Leave it.”

The woodman replied, “Can’t. The wet’s coming through the lower hall.”

Alric glanced at Elianor. She lifted the latch. The guard opened the door a hand’s breadth, and Perran pushed through a small bundle of logs. He was broad-shouldered, mud streaking his boots, his cap pulled low.

He dropped the wood beside the hearth.

“Perran,” Alric said. “You should be below.”

“Aye, my lord.”

Perran knelt and arranged the logs. His hands moved slowly, clumsily, as though he had forgotten how fire worked. When he rose, he looked directly at Elianor.

“Stable roof leaks,” he said.

She understood nothing in the words, yet something in his face told her they were not about the roof.

“How badly?” she asked.

“Bad enough to keep a man awake.”

The guard opened the door wider. “Out.”

Perran bowed. As he passed Elianor, his knuckles brushed the desk. A scrap of cloth remained beneath the edge of the writing board.

The door shut.

Alric stared at her. “What is happening?”

“For the first time,” she said, “people are speaking to one another.”

She waited until his footsteps and the guards’ voices had faded. Then she retrieved the cloth.

It was torn from a stable boy’s sleeve. Sewn into the hem were three short stitches, two long, and three short again.

Nella had shown her the mark on the button. Watching.

This was more.

Elianor held the cloth to the firelight. On its inner fold, written in charcoal, were six words:

THEY KNOW. THEY WILL NOT STAND ALONE.

Her breath caught.

Somewhere beneath the manor, women moved through laundry passages. Stable hands crossed the yard under orders. Kitchen girls lowered their eyes and carried messages in basins. Men who had spent years fearing dismissal, eviction, and the lord’s seal were beginning to measure the locks instead.

It was not an army. It was not yet courage.

It was fear discovering that it had neighbors.

Elianor folded the cloth and hid it inside her sleeve.

At the window, the gallows blurred behind the rain. Dawn was still hours away, but Caelan had made time feel owned, counted out for him like coin.

She placed one blood-marked hand against the glass.

“Tomas,” she whispered.

Behind her, Alric said, “What will you do?”

Elianor looked at the dark courtyard, at the rope waiting beneath the chapel eaves, and at the faint lights moving through Greyfen below.

“What I should have done when he first took the seal,” she said. “I will stop asking permission to resist.”

chapters.name: The Women of Greyfen
chapters.content:
By the second morning, the guards had stopped pretending Elianor’s confinement was temporary.

They brought food at dawn and removed it untouched at noon. Two men stood in the corridor, one outside her door and one beneath the narrow window, where they could watch the chapel roof and the gallows rising beyond it.

The hammering had begun before sunrise.

Each blow traveled through the stone walls. A nail driven. A beam fitted. A death made ready.

Elianor sat beside the dead hearth and listened until the rhythm entered her bones.

On the table lay the wooden button Nella had given her. It was worn smooth by years of use, but a small notch had been carved along its edge.

The women are watching.

She had hidden it beneath her mattress. Then Perran had brought firewood with a cloth concealed among the logs.

They know. They will not stand alone.

It was not a promise of rescue. It was a declaration that fear had ceased to belong to each person separately.

The door opened.

A maid entered carrying a basin, a folded gown, and a basket of linen. Elianor knew her as Jessa, one of the younger laundry girls, though she had never before been permitted to attend her. The girl kept her eyes lowered while the guard watched from the corridor.

“Lady Elianor. Your wedding clothes.”

Elianor looked at the pale blue silk. Silver thread formed thorn branches along its sleeves.

“I have no use for them.”

“The steward says you are to be fitted this afternoon.”

“The steward may fit the gown to himself.”

The guard coughed.

Jessa set down the basket and loosened the top cloth. Beneath the linen lay a gray wool dress and a pair of men’s boots.

Elianor did not move.

“Not now,” Jessa whispered.

“Then when?”

“When the chapel bell rings for the first fitting. The women will be carrying linens up from the lower passage. The guards have been told to watch the main stair.”

“You planned this?”

“All of us.”

The guard shifted outside.

“Who is all?”

Jessa folded the gray dress beneath the blue silk. “Those who have reason.”

She lifted the basin. Before leaving, she said, “Do not eat anything from the steward’s kitchen.”

“Why?”

“Sella is still sick. The steward asked whether she had spoken to you. Nella says the food is being counted twice. Once for you. Once for what it proves.”

The door barred behind her.

At midday the chapel bell rang. A procession of women came up the service stairs carrying sheets, towels, tablecloths, and bolts of wool. They laughed too loudly, filling the corridor with the smell of soap and lavender.

Nella was among them. She dropped a bundle beside the bed.

“Has anyone touched you?” Elianor asked.

“No.”

“Has Caelan questioned you?”

“Everyone.”

“And?”

“I am dull. It is my chief virtue.”

From the bundle she drew the gray dress, a woolen cap, and a narrow knife wrapped in linen.

Elianor took the blade. “If they discover this—”

“They will discover something whether we give them a reason or not.”

The other women began folding curtains and stripping the bed. One was Britha, an old laundress who had served Greyfen for forty years. Another was the kitchen girl who had looked away when Elianor fled through the east passage.

The girl met Elianor’s gaze.

“I did not betray you,” she said.

“I did not say you had.”

“You wondered.”

She folded a sheet with fierce precision. “The guard at the east passage was my brother. They had a rope around his wrist and said they would hang him beside your falconer if he did not tell them which door you used.”

“What did he tell them?”

“That you went through the chapel.”

Elianor thought of the soldiers at the limekiln, of Tomas drawing them away while she hid beneath the earth. She had imagined the betrayal as a willing hand. It was easier to hate that.

Nella pulled the gray dress over Elianor’s head. A strip of linen had been sewn into the waist to flatten her figure and hold papers against her skin. Elianor put on the boots, too large but manageable with thick socks. Nella tucked her hair beneath the cap and darkened her cheeks with hearth soot.

“There,” she said. “You look like a girl who has never owned a mirror.”

“I have owned several.”

“That is why we must improve you.”

The hammer struck below.

Elianor looked through the window. The gallows stood in the courtyard, dark against the snow. Men were raising a rope.

Nella followed her gaze. “We can still get you out.”

“To where?”

“Through the laundry passage, then the orchard. Perran has cut the wire at the old deer gate. There is a cart beyond the lane. It can take you to Fenwatch if the road is clear.”

“And Tomas?”

Nella’s face tightened. “If we take you to him, they will follow. If you go alone, the network can move you.”

“Move me.”

“Hide you. Keep you alive.”
