The word struck Elianor more sharply than the hammering.

Her father had surrendered seals to keep her alive. Tomas had drawn soldiers away to keep her alive. Servants had lied and endured questioning to keep one another alive.

And Tomas would hang in the courtyard so she might be kept alive elsewhere.

“No.”

“My lady—”

“No.”

“You promised him you would cross the marsh.”

“I know.”

“Then let us take you where he wanted you to go.”

“Tomas did not ask me to live while he died.”

“He asked you to live.”

“He asked me to live with him.”

“That may not be possible.”

“No,” Elianor said, watching the gallows. “But I will not make his death the price of my escape.”

Nella seized her wrist. “If you go down there, Caelan may have you dragged beside him. The soldiers may cut through us.”

“Then we face what is coming together.”

“That is grief dressed in a noble coat.”

“It is the first choice I have made that does not require someone else to suffer in my place.”

The women had stopped working.

Britha came forward. “There are men among the wedding workers.”

“What men?”

“Quarry hands. Two from Southmere. A discharged soldier named Harl. They came with the linen wagons yesterday.”

“Rebel sympathizers?”

“People who have stopped waiting for permission.”

“Are they armed?”

“Some.”

“Where is Mara?”

“Perran heard she reached the outer farms,” Jessa said. “She is trying to come through the north road before the snow closes it.”

“She knows what happened?”

“Not yet.”

“Then someone must tell her.”

“Someone will,” Nella said, “if there is someone left to tell.”

Elianor retrieved the button and Perran’s cloth message from beneath the mattress, folding both into the lining of her borrowed dress.

“Where are the estate records?” she asked.

Nella frowned. “What records?”

“The accounts Caelan is using.”

“Locked in the west office.”

“Not all of them. There are duplicate labor books. Southmere’s reeve kept one showing obligations and another showing payments. Caelan has the first. The second may still be in the records room.”

Nella stared at her.

“I want proof,” Elianor said. “Not only for the tenants. For everyone in that courtyard.”

A sound came from the passage. A guard called, “The sheets are counted!”

“Count them again,” Britha shouted. “The steward likes his numbers twice.”

The women laughed. Britha pushed the basket of blue silk toward the door.

They left beneath a mound of white linen. Elianor lay hidden in the cart while Jessa and Britha pushed it through the narrow service passage. Damp stone pressed close on either side. At the mangle room, a guard waited.

“Open it,” he ordered.

“Open it yourself,” Britha replied. “Unless you intend to explain why Lord Caelan’s wedding linens are still wet.”

The guard prodded the basket containing the gray dress.

“These are not linens.”

“They are for the fitting. Would you like to wear them?”

A bucket clattered somewhere behind him. The guard turned toward the noise.

Britha shoved the cart forward.

Elianor slipped out beneath the stairs. Nella followed, then Jessa. The guard was still arguing with Britha.

At the end of the passage stood a warped door. Nella drew out a brass hairpin.

“Locks,” she whispered.

She worked at it, swore, and handed it to Elianor. The lock yielded beneath Elianor’s second attempt.

The records room smelled of dust, leather, and cold iron. Ledgers filled the shelves, marked with the seals of House Vey, Harrowmere, Kestrel Bank, and the Crown timber office.

They searched quickly.

Nella found a bundle tied with red cord. Britha uncovered a thin book whose pages listed labor as payment and payment as arrears. Jessa pulled letters from beneath a loose board.

Elianor opened the first.

By order of Lord Caelan Arbridge, grain withheld until labor deficit is satisfied.

Below it was a list of families, including the Dallows.

The second ordered the dismissal of kitchen girls, grooms, laundry workers, and “Vey loyalists liable to encourage disorder.”

The third bore Alric’s seal but Caelan’s hand.

Secure the estate before the marriage. Any resistance is to be treated as conspiracy.

Elianor tucked the letters into her bodice.

A blow struck the passage door.

Someone had found them.

Britha thrust the ledgers into a canvas sack. Jessa seized the knife. Nella caught Elianor’s shoulder.

“The stable yard is open,” she whispered. “Perran can take you to the deer gate. You can still leave.”

Beyond the walls waited Fenwatch, the marsh, and the difficult life she and Tomas had imagined.

Behind them waited the courtyard, Caelan, and the rope.

Elianor touched the hidden letters.

For years she had believed authority meant preventing harm by choosing who would bear it. She had called that duty. She had called it mercy when the suffering fell on people who could not refuse.

She would not choose again.

“Not the deer gate,” she said.

Nella closed her eyes. “Then where?”

“To the courtyard.”

Another blow shook the door.

Elianor took the knife and tucked it into her belt. She lifted the sack of ledgers.

“Open the main passage. Bring every woman willing to come. Tell the workers to gather by the chapel.”

“And if they are not ready?”

“They are ready enough.”

Britha drew back the bolt.

The door opened onto the passage, where the first guard stood with his hand on his sword.

For one heartbeat, no one moved.

Then Nella stepped beside Elianor. Jessa stepped beside Nella. Behind them, the women filled the narrow hall.

Together they walked toward the courtyard.

chapters.name: The Gallows in the Rain
chapters.content:
By the time the bell began to ring, rain had washed the last snow from the courtyard.

It fell in a fine, needling sheet, darkening the flags and turning the earth to mud. Against the chapel wall stood the gallows, newly built from pale timber. The rope hung beneath its crossbeam, swaying in the wind.

Elianor saw it from the records passage.

Nella stood beside her with an iron bar. Jessa held the canvas sack of ledgers against her chest, while Britha kept one hand pressed over the letter hidden beneath her dress. Behind them crowded women from the laundry, kitchens, and nursery, armed with knives, hooks, stones, or nothing but their courage.

Boots struck the other side of the door.

“Bring him out!” someone shouted.

Nella caught Elianor’s arm. “If we go into the yard, there is no returning.”

“I know.”

“The guards may kill you before you reach him.”

Elianor looked again at the gallows. She remembered Tomas in the forester’s lodge, bending over the injured goshawk with such tenderness. She remembered his voice at the hearing: Do not marry him for my sake.

Too long, she thought, other people had paid for her decisions.

“Then they will have to do it where everyone can see,” she said.

She opened the door.

The courtyard was full: servants, grooms, tenant laborers, kitchen boys, and three nobles beneath the gallery. Two men from Kestrel Bank stood near their horses, clutching leather cases beneath their cloaks.

Lord Alric waited beside the gallows, bareheaded in the rain. He looked diminished, his gray hair plastered to his brow.

Caelan stood near him beneath an umbrella. His black coat was dry, his gloved hand holding a folded paper. His expression hardened when Elianor appeared in a gray servant’s dress and muddy boots.

“Lady Elianor,” he said. “Return to your rooms.”

“Where is he?”

“You have caused sufficient disturbance.”

“Where is Tomas?”

A movement near the chapel drew her gaze. Two soldiers led Tomas into the yard. His wrists were bound before him. His clothes were torn and stiff with mud, one side of his face swollen, blood running again from the wound at his temple.

Behind him came Oren, bent nearly double, his hands tied.

Tomas saw Elianor. Fear crossed his battered face—not for himself, but for her.

“Elianor.”

Caelan stepped between them. “You see the consequence of romantic foolishness. If you return to your rooms, I may yet review the sentence.”

“You sentenced a man to hang because he refused to leave me.”

“I sentenced a trespasser and conspirator under authority granted by your father.”

“Then let my father speak.”

Every face turned toward Alric. His mouth opened, but no words came.

Elianor drew out the letter bearing his seal. Its corners were damp, but the red wax remained intact.

“This bears my father’s seal,” she said, raising it for all to see. “But not his hand. It orders the estate secured before the marriage and says that any resistance is to be treated as conspiracy.”

Caelan’s calm broke. “Give me that.”

She did not move.

“It is a forgery.”

“Then perhaps this is one too.”

Britha stepped forward and opened the sack. She lifted a swollen ledger wrapped in oilcloth.

Caelan’s steward pushed through the crowd.

Nella raised the iron bar.

The steward stopped.

Elianor took the ledger. “This is the original Southmere labor record. It lists the men who repaired the south bridge and the payments owed them. Here is Caelan’s copy, declaring those same men in arrears. Their grain was seized because labor was changed into debt.”

A man beneath the gallery stepped forward. “They took my boat for arrears.”

“And mine,” called another.

“They kept my sons on the north road three weeks.”

The murmurs spread.

Elianor opened another document. “This order withholds grain until labor deficits are satisfied. It names the Dallows of East Hollow. Their cottage was taken after their son fell ill, though they had repaired the south bridge.”

A woman near the kitchens began to weep.

“Elianor,” Alric said.

She looked at him. “You approved it.”

His face tightened with shame.

She turned back to the crowd. “This order records bread sent to the infirmary and north cottages as an advance against six cottages, payable in labor at double rate. Bread for the sick was made into a debt.”

“You understand nothing of accounts,” Caelan said.

“I understand that a starving child cannot eat an entry in a ledger.”

A bitter laugh rose from the tenants.

Caelan swept his gaze over them. “You are witnesses to treason. Anyone who remains with her will be questioned.”

“Questioned how?” Elianor demanded. “As Tomas was? As Oren was? With a cudgel until the answer pleases you?”

Tomas strained against the soldiers. “Do not, Elianor. Get away from here.”

She looked at him. “I have tried.”

Then she raised the ledger above her head.

“This is not stewardship. It is seizure. This is not protection. It is punishment made profitable. They told you each demand was necessary, each eviction the last before better days. But they never meant to preserve your homes. They meant to preserve their right to own you.”

“Silence her!” Caelan shouted.

The guards moved.

Jessa stepped between them and the trough. One struck her shoulder. She staggered. Nella brought the iron bar against his knee, and he fell into the mud.

A stable boy hurled a stone. It struck another guard’s cheek. A kitchen boy pulled the reins from a nobleman’s horse. The animal reared, scattering men beneath the gallery.

A stable hand slammed the western gate shut. Another dropped the iron crossbar into place.

Perran appeared on the mounting block with a short-handled axe. Beside him stood Harl, the discharged soldier, and two Southmere men carrying cudgels. Quarry workers followed from the wagon shed, their hands black with stone dust.

“Greyfen gates are closed!” Perran shouted.

Caelan turned on the nearest soldier. “Open them.”

No one obeyed.

He seized the man’s collar and struck him across the face. The soldier lowered his eyes.

“Open them!”

The man dropped his sword in the mud.

The courtyard roared.

Caelan’s remaining guards lifted their weapons. Harl intercepted the first cudgel meant for him. It cracked against his forearm. He drove the soldier into the chapel wall. The Southmere men rushed the others. A groom threw a bucket into one guard’s wrist, and his blade vanished beneath stamping feet.

Elianor struck the ledger against the stone trough.

“Listen!”

Nella beat the iron bar against it.

Clang. Clang. Clang.

The women took up the cry.

“Listen to Lady Vey!”

The fighting faltered.

Tomas had been forced to his knees. A soldier raised a cudgel over him.

“Stop!” Elianor shouted.

The soldier hesitated.

“He is not your enemy. None of you are paid enough to die for Caelan’s accounts.”

The guard looked around at the workers surrounding him. Slowly, he lowered the cudgel.

Elianor faced the crowd again.

“You know what is written here. You have lived it. You know whose children went hungry, whose labor was counted and then denied. You know who was dismissed for loyalty to House Vey and who was kept because fear made him useful.”

She opened the dismissal list.

“Kitchen girls. Grooms. Laundry workers. Anyone liable to encourage disorder. They meant to dismiss us after the marriage—not because we had failed, but because we had seen too much.”

Jessa’s face went white.

A voice called from the gallery, “Then let them see us now.”

Another gate bar dropped into place.

The nobles shouted for their horses. One Kestrel representative backed toward the hall, clutching his case. Caelan turned toward the chapel as though its stone walls could shelter him.

Then Alric spoke.

“I did not order this.”

Caelan looked at him. “You granted me authority.”

“I granted you use of my seal.”

“You granted me authority over the estate.”

“I did not grant you my daughter.”

“You gave me everything else.”

Alric flinched. He looked toward Tomas, then Oren, who had fallen against the chapel steps.

“I will not hide behind anything,” he said. “Put down your weapons.”

The remaining guards stared at him.

“Put them down.”

For a moment the old order held. Then the nearest guard lowered his sword. Another let his shield fall.

Caelan’s face twisted. “You will hide behind sentiment now?”

“I should have opposed you sooner.”

Caelan turned toward the chapel doors. “Take Lady Elianor. Take her now.”

The soldiers moved, but Harl and the workers closed around them.

Tomas broke free in the confusion. He stumbled against the gallows post, then ran—not after Caelan, but toward Oren. He dragged his father away from the chapel steps and knelt beside him.

“Elianor,” he called. “Get the women out!”

She saw his blood, his shaking hands, the rope hanging above him.

Then the chapel doors burst open.

More of Caelan’s men forced their way into the yard.

Caelan vanished inside.

Tomas looked up at her through the rain. For one breath, the violence fell away. He was alive. She was standing. The rope remained empty.

The chapel bell began ringing again—not from the tower, but within.

A warning. Or a call.

Nella reached Elianor. “He’s alive.”

“I see him.”

Around them, women seized hooks, poles, stones, and broken tools. The stable hands barricaded the main gate. Harl stood with one arm hanging uselessly, gripping a cudgel in the other. The workers gathered beneath the gallows, no longer divided by household, village, or station.

Caelan’s men struck the chapel doors from inside.

The gates shuddered beneath answering blows from outside.

“Stand together!” Harl roared.

Elianor tucked the ledger beneath her coat and faced the chapel. Rain ran into her eyes. Behind her, the women of Greyfen closed ranks. Before her, the house that had ruled them for generations trembled on its foundations.

For the first time in Greyfen’s history, no one waited for permission.

Then the people of the manor struck back.

chapters.name: The Manor Breaks
chapters.content:
The chapel doors shuddered under the weight of the men outside them.

“Stand back!” Harl shouted.

The crowd drew away as a sword thrust through the widening gap. It swept blindly across the threshold and cut a stable boy high in the arm. He fell, clutching the wound.

The yard answered with a roar.

Harl seized the sword arm and dragged it down. Three men slammed against the doors. From within came Caelan’s voice, calm even through the tumult.

“Drive them back! Any man who lowers his weapon is to be hanged with the rest.”

The threat had once possessed the force of law. Now it was only a voice behind wood.

Perran kicked the injured boy’s fallen knife toward the stable hands. “Get him to the kitchens.”

“I can walk,” the boy gasped.

“You can bleed there.”

The women carried him away. Nella had one hand pressed against Jessa’s shoulder, where a cudgel had struck her, and the other wrapped around the iron bar she had used in the courtyard.

“Where is Tomas?” Britha demanded.

Elianor looked toward the chapel steps.

Tomas was kneeling beside Oren. The old falconer had collapsed on one elbow, gray hair plastered to his face by rain. Tomas cut through the ropes at his wrists with a stolen knife. Blood darkened his coat.

Elianor’s heart lurched.

Then Oren tried to rise, and Tomas caught him.

“I’m here,” he said. “Easy, Da. I’ve got you.”

Oren’s eyes found Elianor. He tried to speak, but only a raw breath escaped.

“Take him to the infirmary,” she called.

Tomas looked across the yard at her.

She wanted to run to him, but the chapel doors groaned again, and men shouted at the western gate.

“I’ll bring him,” Tomas said.

“No. Take him through the scullery passage. Nella will open the infirmary.”

His expression tightened. He understood that she was asking him to carry the wounded away from the fight.

“You?”

“The armory.”

“You know the way?”

“I was born here.”

“That has never stopped them locking doors.”

“It may stop them knowing which doors are false.”

For one instant, despite the blood and rain, his face softened. Then he turned, supporting Oren toward the kitchens.

Elianor watched him go until Nella seized her sleeve.

“If you mean to reach the armory, you’ll need more than a family name.”

She thrust a ring of keys into Elianor’s hand.

“Where did you get these?”

“Master Pell’s belt.”

“Is Pell alive?”

“He was when I took them.”

Another crash shook the chapel. The crowd surged backward.

“Move,” Nella said. “Before the house decides for us.”

Elianor crossed the yard with Nella, Britha, Perran, Harl, and six stable hands around her. Rain had turned the straw beneath their boots into yellow paste. Smoke drifted from the eastern wing. Men ran in every direction, shouting orders or names.

A kitchen boy came sprinting from the storehouse with a sack of flour over his shoulder, followed by two guards who had abandoned their helmets.

“The stores are open!” he cried. “The grain is ours!”

“It is not yours to scatter,” Perran said.

The boy stopped, frightened.

Perran lowered his voice. “Count it. Bring the ledgers if you can. No one takes more than their household needs.”

“They’ll starve us again.”

“Not if we know what there is.”

He turned to the others. “Make lists. Every sack and barrel. If we live through this, those lists will matter.”

Even now, Elianor thought, he was making an account—not for a lord or creditor, but for the people who had carried Greyfen through winter.

Two guards blocked the covered passage.

“Lady Elianor,” said the one in Vey colors, “you cannot go inside.”

“I can, and I will.”

“His lordship ordered—”

“His lordship has no authority here.”

The guard glanced toward the chapel. “Lord Alric—”

“Lord Alric declared Caelan’s orders forged.”

That made him hesitate. The other guard drew his sword.

Harl struck it aside with a length of firewood. Britha drove her shoulder into the man’s chest, and both fell. The Vey guard raised his hands.

“I have no quarrel with you.”

“Then step aside.”

He did.

Inside, Greyfen had become a maze of noise. Doors stood open. Servants hauled furniture against entrances and carried water toward the eastern wing. Somewhere above, glass shattered.

Elianor led them through the old laundry corridor, past the disused washhouse and down the narrow stair beneath the household chapel. She had discovered the passage as a child while hiding from her governess. Its entrance lay behind a panel carved with the Vey stag.

She tried the third brass key. It failed. The fourth stuck. The fifth turned.

The panel opened onto darkness and cold earth.

“Stay close,” she said.

They descended. Water dripped from the ceiling into channels between the stones. Behind them, boots struck the stair.

The group pressed into alcoves as three men hurried past the hidden entrance. Caelan’s steward was among them.

“Search the west rooms,” he ordered. “The records first. His lordship wants the records.”

Elianor closed her hand around the keys.

“He knows,” she whispered.

“He has known for some time,” Nella replied. “Now he has reason to fear them.”

When the footsteps faded, they continued. The passage emerged behind the old armory.

Two soldiers were overturning racks of spears.

“Stay where you are!” one shouted.

Perran threw a brick. It struck the man’s wrist. Harl and the stable hands rushed them. The fight was brief and ugly. When it ended, one soldier lay senseless beneath the rack. The other dropped his sword and held his split lip.

“Take the weapons,” Elianor said.

The stable hands stared at her.

“Take them. Give the Vey guards a choice. Those who stand with Caelan are to be disarmed. Those who surrender are to be bound, not butchered.”

Harl looked at her, then nodded.

They opened the armory. There were a dozen short swords, hunting bows, axes, and old mail shirts. The workers took what they could carry. Perran distributed the blades carefully.

Pounding sounded from the corridor.

“More men,” Britha said.

Elianor pointed to the second door. It led to the records room through a service stair.

“Go. Get the books out. Put them where the tenants can see them.”

“And you?” Nella asked.

“I’ll hold this door.”

“You have a talent for choosing the worst place to stand.”

“I learned from watching my father.”

Nella swore under her breath and led the others away.

The first blow struck the armory door. Dust fell from the lintel.

“Lady Elianor,” called the steward. “Open the door. There is still time to prevent bloodshed.”

“There was time,” she answered. “You spent it.”

The next blow came with an axe.

Before the door could break, another shout rose from the corridor.

“Drop it!”

Elianor recognized her father’s voice.

Through a splintered gap she saw Alric standing beneath the archway, a pistol held in both hands. He looked small in his soaked dressing coat. Four Vey guards stood behind him; one had lowered his sword, another was bleeding from the forehead.

The steward raised his axe. “You gave us the order to secure the house.”

“I gave no order to attack the women.”

“You gave Caelan your seal.”

Alric flinched.

From the far corridor came a scream. Kitchen workers fled toward them, pursued by six of Caelan’s men. One guard dragged a fallen girl backward by the hair. Another carried a torch.

“Close the door!” Alric shouted.

The soldier raised his sword over the girl.

Alric fired.

The shot thundered through the corridor. The soldier dropped. Smoke rolled beneath the ceiling.

The steward stared at Alric. “You’ve chosen.”

“Yes,” Alric said.

He rushed forward as the steward swung. The pistol clicked empty. Alric caught the axe blade with both hands. It cut into his palms, but he held it fast.

“Run,” he told the workers.

They ran.

Elianor shoved open the armory door and joined the fight. She did not remember drawing the short sword. She remembered the steward’s axe rising and Nella’s iron bar crashing into his knee. He fell with a howl. Britha kicked the weapon away.

The remaining men broke. Some fled toward the great hall; others threw down their swords.

“Bind them!” Elianor ordered. “Every man who surrenders.”

A flour-covered woman seized a fallen soldier’s belt and tied his wrists. “And if they come back?”

“Then we will know who they are.”

She looked dissatisfied, but obeyed.

Alric stood amid the wreckage, staring at the man he had shot.

“I should have done it sooner,” he said.

Elianor lowered her sword. “Yes.”

He looked at her, seeking the forgiveness she could not give.

“Where is Caelan?” she asked.

“Inside the chapel, I think. Or the west hall. His men are trying to reach the records.”

“Then we must reach them first.”

“The records room?”

“And the armory. We have weapons now.”

A tremor moved through him. “You do not understand what follows. If Caelan is harmed, Arbridge will send soldiers. The Crown will call this treason. Every lord in Valedorn—”

“Will call it treason whether we live quietly or die loudly.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one you taught me.”

The chapel doors gave way in the courtyard. A roar swept through the house.

Then men appeared at the far archway, retreating from the chapel and dragging one of the Kestrel representatives between them. The banker’s fine coat was torn, and blood marked his temple. At their center walked Caelan, immaculate except for rain on his shoulders.

He stopped when he saw Alric.

“Put down the pistol,” Caelan said.

“It is empty.”

“Then put down your authority.”

Alric straightened.

Caelan glanced at Elianor. “You have made your choice plain. You will not make this household your shield.”

“This household is no longer yours to command.”

“It belongs to the person who can hold it.”

He nodded to his men.

They moved toward the kitchen workers.

Alric stepped between them. “No.”

“Stand aside.”

“No.”

One of Caelan’s men struck Alric across the face with a sword hilt. He staggered into the wall.

Caelan’s men surged forward. The Vey guards closed around Alric, and servants seized whatever lay near—bars, knives, broken chair legs. The corridor became a knot of bodies and shouting.

Perran pulled the banker away from his captors. Nella struck a man in the throat. Britha opened the records passage and shouted for the others to carry what they could.

Caelan backed toward the west hall.

Elianor saw him searching for an escape.

“You will not leave,” she said.

He met her eyes. “You think this is victory?”

“No.”

“Then you are wiser than your father.”

He disappeared through the archway. A moment later, the west doors slammed shut.

No one followed. The corridor was full of injured men, broken weapons, and servants breathing as though they had run miles. Beyond the walls, Greyfen continued to cry out—at the stores, the gates, the stables, the chapel. Every locked room was being opened. Every order was being questioned.

Alric sank against the wall, blood running from his mouth.

Elianor knelt beside him, though she did not touch him.

“Are you badly hurt?”

He looked at his hands. “Not badly enough.”

Around them, the household moved without waiting for permission. Keys passed from palm to palm. Weapons were counted. Prisoners were bound. The records emerged from the hidden stair in armfuls, their leather covers darkening in the rain.

Greyfen had stood for generations because everyone inside it had known where to stand: lord above servant, master above tenant, command above obedience.

Now those lines had broken.

The manor did not fall in one crash. It broke room by room, door by door, hand by hand, until no one could say where the old authority ended and the people began.

Elianor rose and took the first ledger from Perran.

“Bring the rest,” she said.

Behind them, the west doors shook.

Ahead, the records room waited in darkness.

chapters.name: The Burning Ledgers
chapters.content:
The records room lay beyond the west gallery, behind a door swollen by damp and barred from within.

Elianor knew the passage because she had been forbidden to use it as a child. Her father had called accounts the bones of a house and told her bones were not beautiful when brought into the light.

Now smoke curled beneath the door.

“Back,” Perran warned.

He raised the stolen sword. Behind them, the manor shook with fighting: boots on stone, a woman shouting, furniture breaking against a door. Tomas stood at the rear, one arm around his father’s waist. Oren’s feet dragged, and every breath rattled. Tomas’s shirt was dark with blood beneath the ribs.

Elianor looked at him. “You should be in the infirmary.”

“So should half the people in this house.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the one I have.”

Oren made a faint sound, and Tomas tightened his hold.

Nella stepped forward with a broken poker. “We cannot argue while Caelan burns the proof.”

Perran drove his shoulder into the door. The bar cracked but held. On the second blow, the hinges screamed and the door burst inward.

Heat rolled over them.

Two men in Kestrel livery were throwing papers into a brazier. A third had overturned a chest and was feeding handfuls of parchment to the flames. The room’s shutters trapped smoke beneath the ceiling. Ledgers stood along the walls, their leather spines filmed with mildew.

The nearest man reached for a pistol.

Perran crossed the room before he could raise it. His sword struck the weapon aside, and Nella’s poker caught the man across the wrist. Britha flung a stool into the knees of the second. The third stumbled backward, clutching a ledger.

“Do not kill them,” Elianor said.

Perran’s sword hovered at the fallen man’s throat. “They were burning the records.”

“Bind them.”

The men were stripped of their weapons and tied to the legs of an overturned table. One had blood running from his mouth. He stared at Elianor as though she were the one who had become monstrous.

She knelt beside the brazier. Beneath the burning sheets lay a thick ledger whose leather cover had blackened without catching. She dragged it free with the poker.

The title, written in a faded clerk’s hand, read: SOUTHMERE—LABOR AND ARREARS, 41 YEARS.

Her fingers tightened.

“Take out the ash,” she ordered. “Save what can be read.”

Perran overturned the brazier into a brass basin. Jessa and Britha stamped out the sparks while Nella opened the shutters. Rain struck the glass and turned the smoke into a low gray veil.

Elianor opened the ledger.

Names filled the pages: cottages, fields, boats, marsh strips. Beside each were columns of grain advanced, labor owed, interest added, penalties carried forward. At first the figures appeared orderly. Then she saw the same debt repeated year after year, though the labor beside it had been marked complete.

Paid in full, witnessed by reeve.

The next line added the payment to the following year’s arrears.

“Here,” she whispered.

Nella came beside her. “What is it?”

“They counted the same labor twice.”

“More than twice,” Tomas said.

He had guided Oren to a chair. He leaned against the frame, pale and watchful. “Look at the dates. The road crews were credited as unpaid in winter, then charged again when they repaired the summer bridges.”

Elianor turned the pages. He was right. One year became the next, and the debt became a chain that lengthened with every attempt to break it.

A heavy blow struck the west doors. The walls trembled.

“Elianor,” Perran said. “We have minutes.”

She looked around the room. For generations, a stroke of a pen had evicted families, seized boats, turned bread into debt, and made free people labor without wages. The papers did not look powerful. They looked like the remains of a lie.

“Bring them out,” she said.

Nella stared at the shelves. “All?”

“As many as can be carried. Separate Southmere, the mill accounts, timber, and cottage leases.”

“What do we do with the rest?”

“Make copies. Names, dates, seals, amounts. Enough that no one can call it rumor.”

She crossed to the writing desk. Ink had spilled across it, but three pens remained in a jar. She spread blank account sheets over the wood.

“Now?” Jessa asked. “While men are breaking down the house?”

“I want them to find that the house has already been opened.”

The ledgers were carried into the gallery. Tenant representatives had begun gathering there: Southmere men, quarry workers, two women from East Hollow, and a miller with a bandage around his head. They stood with weapons in their hands, staring at the books.

Elianor laid the first ledger open on the floor.

“Read your names.”

No one moved.

An old man from Southmere crouched beside it. His finger followed the lines.

“That is my father,” he said. “He owed three days for the west ditch.”

“According to this, he owed thirty-seven.”

“He worked the ditch.”

“I know.”

“My brother worked it after him.”

“So did you.”

The old man looked up. “Then who owes it?”

Elianor turned the page. “Here are the boat seizures and grain penalties. Here is the labor book with payments recorded, and here is the duplicate in which those payments vanish.”

The miller bent over the pages. “This mark is the reeve’s.”

“And this?” asked one of the women.

“Caelan’s steward,” Elianor said. “This seal is my father’s.”

A murmur passed through the corridor.

Alric’s seal. Caelan’s hand.

The truth pressed against Elianor like a stone. Her father had not written the orders, but he had lent the authority that made them dangerous. The seal spoke in his name because he had allowed another man to hold it.

Tomas watched her from the wall.

She wanted to touch him, to make certain he was still there. Instead, he pressed his palm to his wounded side and looked toward the stair.

“Caelan is moving,” he said.

A breathless groom appeared at the far end of the gallery. “Toward the chapel. Six or seven with him. Maybe more. They have weapons.”

“And the gates?”

“Still barred. Some of his men are trying to get through the lower court.”

Tomas pushed away from the wall.

Elianor caught his wrist. “No.”

“We have to open the manor gates.”

“Perran can do it.”

“Perran has to hold the records. People are trapped between the house and the outer wall. Kitchen girls, stable hands, the men who surrendered. If Caelan reaches them, he will use them to force the gates.”

“Then we stop him here.”

“This room is not the battle.”

“It is the proof.”

“And proof is useless if everyone carrying it is dead.”

The words struck because she had thought the same thing.

Tomas glanced toward Oren. The old falconer had slid lower in his chair. Britha knelt beside him, binding his shoulder with a strip torn from a tablecloth.

“He needs the infirmary,” Tomas said.

“So do you.”

“I can still walk.”

“That is a poor measure of life.”

“It is the only one we have.”

Another blow came from the west side of the manor. Dust sifted from the ceiling.

Elianor returned to the records room. The brazier had gone dark, but smoke lingered in the air. She lifted a taper from the desk and held it over the nearest ledger.

Tomas followed. “What are you doing?”

“If Caelan takes the room, he takes the records.”

“We can carry them.”

“Not all. And his men will burn what they cannot save.”

She touched the taper to a ledger.

The leather resisted. Then the dry pages caught, and a thin blue flame ran along the margin.

“Some of these are the only record,” Tomas said.

“We have written what matters.”

“Not everything.”

“Then let them be the last record of the world that made them.”

She set fire to another book, then another. Flames climbed the shelves. Inked names curled and vanished. The ledgers collapsed into sparks and ash.

Elianor thought of the families named in them: those expelled, those who had died repairing roads, those who had paid debts that never ended. The fire did not distinguish guilt from suffering. It only erased the weapon.

The manor shook. From below came a roar of voices, then the crack of a musket.

“Go,” Elianor told Tomas.

He did not move.

“Tomas.”

“I am not leaving you.”

“You are going to the gates.”

“No.”

“Take Perran and Harl. Open them. Get the servants out before Caelan reaches the courtyard.”

“And you?”

“I will bring the records to the tenant representatives.”

“You said you would not disappear from me.”

“I said I would not disappear. I am telling you where I will be.”

The fire snapped behind her.

He came close enough for her to see the exhaustion beneath his eyes. “You cannot go toward Caelan.”

“I am not going toward him.”

“You know he will come for you.”

“I know.”

“Then stay with me.”

Her courage nearly failed at the simplicity of it.

“If I stay, the people behind us remain trapped,” she said. “If you stay, the same is true. We cannot keep choosing each other in ways that leave everyone else to Caelan.”

His face tightened. “I know what you are asking.”

“I am asking you to trust me.”

“I have trusted you with my life since the first day you brought linen to the lodge.”

“And I have trusted you with mine.”

“Then do not make me spend it watching you walk into fire.”

“I will not walk into fire. I will carry what the fire cannot destroy.”

The manor shook again.

Tomas closed his eyes for one heartbeat. When he opened them, fear remained, but something steadier stood beside it.

“Promise me,” he said.

“What?”

“If you reach a choice between saving me and saving them, you will save them. Do not trade yourself for me.”

She shook her head. “I cannot promise that.”

“You can.”

“I will not make a promise I may break.”

His hand rose and touched her cheek. “Then promise me you will try.”

She covered his hand with hers. “And if you reach a choice between killing Caelan and saving prisoners?”

His gaze faltered.

“You will save the prisoners,” she said.

A silence passed between them, filled with rain, fire, and the pounding at the doors.

“Yes,” he said.

“Then yes.”

He bent and kissed her. It was brief and fierce, tasting of blood. When he pulled away, he rested his forehead against hers.

“Do not make me regret teaching you to disobey.”

“You taught me nothing. I was disobedient before I met you.”

For one impossible instant, they smiled.

Then Tomas turned toward the gallery. “Perran. Harl. With me.”

They gathered weapons and hurried after him. Oren stirred as Tomas passed.

“Boy,” the old falconer whispered.

Tomas stopped.

“Open… the sky.”

Tomas knelt, pressed his brow to his father’s, and rose.

Elianor watched him go.

Nella came to her side with a bundle of copied pages beneath her dress. “We have to move.”

“I know.”

The fire had reached the upper shelves, throwing fierce gold across the room. Elianor seized the last Southmere ledger, the forged letter, the grain order, and the dismissal list. She tucked them beneath her cloak.

Behind her, the records of House Vey collapsed into flame.

At the end of the gallery, a shout rose.

“The gates!”

For one moment it sounded like victory.

Then another voice cried, “Caelan’s men are at the chapel!”

Elianor looked toward the passage where Tomas had vanished. Beyond the walls, rain lashed the courtyard. The gallows rope swung empty in the storm.

She gathered the ledgers against her chest and ran.

chapters.name: Dawn at Greyfen
chapters.content:
The chapel bell rang without a hand upon it.

A fire had caught the rope in the loft, and whenever wind drove smoke through the broken windows, the bell lurched and tolled across Greyfen. Its sound carried over the burning records room, the shattered west hall, and the cries of men calling for water, weapons, or mercy.

Tomas reached the lower gate with Perran and Harl. Beyond it, servants and surrendered soldiers were trapped between the wall and Caelan’s remaining men. Harl worked at the bar while Perran held the passage.

“You’re bleeding through again,” Harl said.

“It can wait.”

“It has been waiting since the gallows.”

“So have they.”

Tomas put his shoulder against the doors. Pain tore beneath his ribs, but he drove forward with Harl. The doors opened onto rain, and the prisoners stumbled through—some carrying children, some dragging the wounded. A guard threw down his sword before crossing the threshold.

Perran seized him.

“No killing,” Tomas said.

“He was one of them.”

“He’s unarmed now.”

Perran’s fury held for a moment, then he shoved the guard toward the stable hands, who bound him with reins.

“More at the west gate,” Harl said. “And Caelan’s gone toward the chapel.”

Tomas looked back at the manor. Flames shone through the records wing roof, turning the rain copper. Somewhere within that burning house Elianor carried the evidence of all they had endured.

He ran.

The chapel doors stood open. Candles had fallen among the rushes, and fire crawled beneath the pews. At the altar, Caelan held a pistol in one hand and a leather case in the other. Two armed men guarded him. A third lay motionless near the font.

Caelan glanced at Tomas.

“I had expected you to be dead.”

“I’ve disappointed you before.”

Perran and Harl entered with stable hands and three soldiers who had deserted Caelan. Caelan’s gaze moved over them, offended rather than frightened.

“You’ve let the rabble loose,” he said.

“You did that yourself.”

“This case contains contracts bearing lawful seals. Claims recognized by the banks and the Crown. Burn the manor and you burn your own protection.”

“Give it to us.”

Caelan raised the pistol toward Tomas. “Stand aside. You can still leave. I’ll have you hanged only if you insist on making a spectacle of yourself.”

“You sentenced me to hang for walking beside the woman I love.”

“For trespass, conspiracy, theft of arms, and attempted abduction.”

“For refusing to belong to you.”

Caelan’s expression hardened. “Nothing belongs to a man until it is secured. That is the difference between one who governs and one who dreams.”

He shifted the pistol.

Tomas stepped forward. One of Caelan’s men raised his sword, but Harl struck it aside. Perran rushed the other guard. The chapel erupted, yet Caelan’s arm remained steady.

Tomas could kill him. One stroke beneath the ribs, and the fear might end.

Then he remembered Oren beneath the kitchen stairs, barely breathing as he whispered, Open the sky.

Tomas let his sword fall.

Perran stared. “Tomas—”

“No.” Tomas kept his eyes on Caelan. “We will not build what comes next from the same hunger that built this. You believe everything can be owned if a seal is pressed upon it. You believe fear is the only thing keeping people from becoming beasts.”

Caelan’s mouth tightened.

“If I kill you because I hate you,” Tomas said, “then you are right about us.”

“You sanctimonious fool.”

Caelan fired.

The shot struck Tomas below the ribs. At first there was only the force of it, folding him inward. Then warmth spread beneath his coat, and the chapel tipped sideways.

Elianor screamed his name.

Harl threw himself at Caelan’s pistol arm. Perran cut down one guard, then stopped before striking again. The deserters forced the remaining man to his knees. Caelan wrestled free and ran through the side door, leaving the leather case open on the floor.

Elianor reached Tomas as he sank against a pew.

“No.”

“It missed anything important.”

“Don’t lie.”

Her hands pressed against his wound. Blood pushed between her fingers.

Behind her, Caelan slammed Harl against a pillar. Perran seized him, but Caelan tore free.

“The prisoners,” Tomas said.

Elianor stared at him.

“Get them out.”

“I’m not leaving you.”

“You’re going to open the way.”

She understood. She bent and kissed his forehead.

“Stay alive.”

“I’ll try.”

She rose and shouted, “To the outer gate! Everyone who can walk, move now!”

Tomas pushed himself upright and followed.

Rain fell harder in the courtyard. Fire ran along the gallery roof, sending steam upward. At the gatehouse, Caelan shouted through the bars to armed men gathering beyond the wall.

“Open the gate, and I’ll spare those inside!”

Elianor was already at the winch, fighting its jammed chain. Nella carried Sella wrapped in a blanket. Britha led Oren in a chair, one hand steadying his shoulder. His breath rattled, but he lived.

Tomas saw him and nearly smiled.

Oren lifted one shaking hand.

“Open,” he whispered.

“The sky,” Tomas answered.

The winch groaned. The gate rose by inches.

Caelan saw Tomas. “You still have time. Stop this, and I’ll have the surgeon attend you.”

“You shot me.”

“You forced my hand.”

“You always say that.”

Caelan drew a dagger from his sleeve and lunged toward Elianor.

Tomas moved. He caught Caelan’s arm and drove him against the gatehouse wall. The dagger struck stone.

“You should have killed me,” Caelan hissed.

“Yes,” Tomas said. “But I’m still trying not to.”

Caelan drove his knee into Tomas’s wound. Pain burst through him. He fell, and Caelan wrenched free.

Perran struck Caelan across the jaw with the flat of his sword. Caelan dropped to one knee. Harl kicked the dagger away.

“Bind him,” Elianor ordered.

A stable hand came forward with rope.

“You’ll hang for this,” Caelan spat.

“No,” Elianor said. “You will answer for it.”

The gate rose high enough for people to crawl beneath. Servants began pushing through—kitchen workers, laundry women, tenants, children, wounded soldiers. Some carried grain sacks. Some carried nothing. All crossed into the rain.

Elianor remained at the winch.

“Go,” Tomas told her.

“I’m waiting for you.”

“Then wait outside.”

“I will not.”

A crack split the air. Part of the records wing collapsed inward, sending burning beams through the roof. The chapel bell gave one final, broken toll.

Lord Alric appeared beneath the archway. Blood soaked his coat, and one arm hung uselessly at his side. He looked from Caelan to the open gate.

“Take them out,” he said.

“Come with us,” Elianor answered.

He stared at Greyfen—the burning roofs, the broken windows, the gardens drowned beneath ash and rain.

“I have spent my life keeping the house standing,” he said. “I don’t know how to leave it.”

“You don’t have to save it.”

“No. I should have learned that sooner.”

A figure moved behind him in the smoke. One of Caelan’s men, thought dead, raised a sword. Alric turned. The blade struck beneath his shoulder.

He seized the soldier and drove him backward into the flames. Then he fell against the arch.

Elianor ran to him.

“Father.”

His face had gone gray beneath the soot. He looked toward the people crossing the gate.

“I thought obedience was the same as love,” he whispered. “I was wrong.”

His fingers closed weakly around hers.

“Get them clear.”

“I can’t leave you.”

“You must.”

His hand loosened.

Elianor bowed over it, then rose.

Tomas stood a few paces away, swaying. Perran had dragged Caelan into the road, where Mara and armed villagers were arriving through the rain. At their sight, the remaining Arbridge men threw down their weapons.

“Everyone out!” Elianor called.

Tomas tried to reach the gate. His knees failed.

She caught him as he fell.

“I have you.”

“No, you don’t.”

“I do.”

They sank beneath the gatehouse, rain falling through the broken roof. Around them, the survivors moved toward the woods. Harl called that the wall was clear. Nella shouted for blankets. Perran urged the wounded onward.

“Did they all get out?” Tomas asked.

“Everyone we could find.”

“Oren?”

“Alive. Mara has him.”

He closed his eyes.

“Good.”

Elianor pulled his head into her lap. Blood soaked her skirt. She pressed the wound, though they both knew it was useless.

“You promised,” she said.

“I promised to try.”

“You promised you wouldn’t disappear.”

“I’m right here.”

“That isn’t enough.”

His breath shuddered. “It has to be.”

Beyond the gate, the rain softened. Dawn paled the road and the faces gathered there. Greyfen still burned, but the flames had begun to sink.

A goshawk appeared above the ridge.

It circled once, its wing uneven but strong, then climbed into the brightening sky.

“Oren will be pleased,” Tomas murmured.

“It came back.”

“Perhaps it wanted to see the sky.”

She bent over him. “Stay until the rain stops.”

“It won’t.”

“Then stay until morning.”

“It is morning.”

She looked down. His breathing had grown shallow.

“I love you,” she said.

His eyes opened once more.

“I know.”

“You should say it.”

“I love you,” he whispered. “Enough to let you go.”

“I don’t want to go.”

“You must.”

His hand tightened once around hers.

“Take them somewhere the gates don’t close,” he said. “Don’t build a statue for me, Elianor. Build a door.”

Her tears fell onto his face.

“I will.”

He looked toward the road, where the people of Greyfen were disappearing into the rain.

Then he breathed out, and did not breathe again.

Elianor held him beneath the open gate while Greyfen smoldered behind them. Above the ruined manor, the goshawk circled once more, and dawn came through the clouds.

chapters.name: What Remains
chapters.content:
By noon, the rain had washed the blood from the stones, but it could not wash Greyfen clean.

Smoke lay over the hill in long gray bands. The records wing had collapsed inward, taking half the west roof with it. The chapel stood open to the weather, its bell silent above the blackened rafters. Windows gaped along the manor’s lower floor, and where the great doors had been there was only a warped frame and a scatter of iron hinges.

Elianor sat beneath the broken archway with Tomas’s coat around her shoulders.

It was still damp from the rain and smelled of woodsmoke, horse, and him.

Mara had asked her twice to come down to the woods. The others were gathering there: servants, tenants, wounded men, children carried beneath cloaks. Those who could walk were helping those who could not. The dead had been laid beneath the yew trees, wrapped in blankets when blankets could be spared.

Elianor had not moved.

Tomas lay beside her beneath a sheet borrowed from the laundry. His face had become peaceful in death, though there was soot along one cheek and blood dried beneath his ribs. His hand rested palm upward, as if waiting for hers even now.

She held it until the warmth left him.

Above the ruined roofline, the goshawk circled once. Its flight was not straight. One wing still dipped lower than the other, but it held the air.

Elianor watched it climb until the gray sky swallowed it.

Then she rose.

The first thing she did was open the stores.

The keys had been recovered from the steward’s office, blackened but usable. The grain room was half empty, though Caelan’s men had intended to reserve the remaining sacks for the creditors’ arrival. Elianor stood before them while the frightened storekeeper, Britha, and three tenant women watched.

“Everything goes out,” Elianor said.

Britha looked toward the doorway. “My lady, if the Crown comes—”

“The Crown may eat its warrants.”

No one laughed. The words sounded too much like Tomas, and the memory struck her with such force that she had to brace one hand against the wall.

Mara came in carrying a bloodstained bandage. “We have two days before the wounded must move again. Less, if Arbridge riders come from the south.”

“Then send word to every village that Greyfen’s stores are open. No account of labor. No pledges. No taking names.”

Britha stared at her.

Elianor took the ring of keys from the storekeeper’s shaking hand and placed it in hers. “If they come with hunger, feed them. If they come with weapons, give them what can be spared. If anyone tries to close the doors, send for me.”

That afternoon, the people of East Hollow came up the hill.

The Dallows arrived with their sick son bundled between them. Southmere followed with marsh laborers, boatmen, and two families who had slept three nights in a ruined cart shed. Men from the mill brought flour dust on their sleeves. The dismissed grooms came carrying shovels. Even some of Caelan’s surviving guards appeared without weapons, too ashamed or too frightened to look directly at the women who had bound them.

Elianor gave them grain, salt, lamp oil, blankets, and the contents of the winter stores. She gave them the horses Caelan had meant to claim and the timber he had meant to sell. She ordered the empty cottages opened, then walked through them herself, marking broken shutters and collapsed hearths.

No one called her lady in those days.

They called her Elianor, or simply asked where to carry things.

She preferred it.

Caelan was taken to Fenwatch under guard before the second night. He went in a locked wagon, his wrists chained, the leather case strapped beneath the driver’s seat. He had demanded a magistrate, a priest, and the immediate return of property unlawfully withheld from him.

“You are my wife-to-be,” he had told Elianor at the gate, before Mara’s villagers dragged him away. “Everything you possess remains mine by contract.”

Elianor had looked at the burned chapel behind him.

“No,” she said. “Not anymore.”

The contracts traveled with him, but so did the copies of the ledgers. So did the bound Kestrel men who had survived the fire. So did the testimony of servants, tenants, and soldiers who had heard Caelan order the execution.

The wider rebellion had already reached the roads. By the time Caelan was brought before a court in Fenwatch, three other estates had risen, and the Crown’s officers were divided between offering pardons and ordering reprisals. Caelan’s case became too useful to bury and too dangerous to settle quickly.

He claimed that Greyfen had been lawfully secured through debt. He claimed Elianor was deranged by grief. He claimed Tomas had plotted her abduction.

Then Britha testified about the grain room.

The Dallows testified about East Hollow.

The millers produced duplicate entries showing that labor marked paid had been counted again as arrears. Mara brought witnesses from Southmere, and the Kestrel men, fearing they would hang beside Caelan, admitted that the forged accounts had been prepared under his instruction.

The court did not ask whether a lord could be cruel. It asked whether cruelty had been properly recorded.

That question took months to answer.

Caelan survived the first winter. He survived the collapse of the old provincial council. He survived the execution of two Arbridge captains and the burning of three creditor offices. Whether he would survive the judgment remained uncertain when spring came.

Elianor did not attend his hearings.

She had too much to do at Greyfen.

The manor could not be restored as it had been. Its west wing was unsafe, the chapel roof was gone, and the great hall filled with rain whenever the wind turned east. The estate’s debts remained, though some were declared fraudulent and others transferred to the new authority that had risen in the rebellion’s wake.

There were letters from Harrowmere demanding payment.

There were notices from Kestrel Bank claiming the mill and north silver tract.

There were Crown officers asking for timber rights, inventories, and proof that Elianor had not aided treason.

She answered them all from a room above the kitchens because it was the only part of the house with an unbroken roof.

Greyfen was no longer a manor, she wrote. It was a refuge under public protection.

The first time an officer arrived to seize the mill, he found forty families standing across the bridge with tools in their hands. The second time, he found copies of the forged accounts posted on every gate from Greyfen to Fenwatch. The third time, Mara met him on the road with a letter signed by three villages and a rebel council whose soldiers outnumbered his.

He left without taking anything.

After that, Elianor began selling the estate.

She sold the silver tract first, though it had never yielded silver enough to justify its name. The proceeds repaired the south bridge and bought seed. She sold the timber license to a cooperative of millers and charcoal burners, who agreed to replant what they cut. She sold the eastern pasture to the families who had worked it for generations, accepting payment in small shares rather than a single impossible sum.

Alric’s portrait was taken down from the great hall before the wall collapsed.

Elianor kept it.

She could not forgive him completely. She did not wish to forget what fear had made of him. But when she looked at the painted face—tired eyes, careful mouth, the proud dark coat of a man determined to be remembered as a lord—she saw also the father who had once carried her through a fever and the man who had died refusing to leave the house he had failed to save.

He had mistaken obedience for love.

She would not make the same mistake.

The remaining Vey lands were reorganized in the second year. Her seal was placed on the decree abolishing hereditary service. No child would inherit a master because of the cottage into which he or she had been born. No tenant could be charged labor beyond the season’s agreed levy. Grain issued in hunger would not become a debt without written consent, witnessed by the village council.

The old stewards objected.

One called it madness. Another called it theft. A third reminded Elianor that her ancestors had governed Greyfen for four hundred years.

“Then they had four hundred years to learn better,” she replied.

She worked with Mara and the leaders of the marsh villages to establish courts in which tenants could challenge seizures, evictions, and labor claims. The first court met in Greyfen’s roofless hall. Rain fell through the rafters while a former bailiff stood before the bench and listened to a woman from Southmere describe the seizure of her boat.

The bailiff protested that no noble court would have heard such a complaint.

“This is not a noble court,” Mara said.

Elianor sat among the witnesses rather than above them.

That distinction mattered. It mattered when a miller accused a former soldier. It mattered when a tenant accused Elianor’s own steward of withholding seed. It mattered when the court ordered Greyfen to return land that had been wrongly claimed by the Vey family generations before.

Elianor signed the order.

The steward looked at her as if she had cut off her own hand.

Perhaps she had.

Nobles called her traitor. Some said she had murdered her father by leading the uprising. Others said she had disgraced her blood, slept with a servant, and handed a noble estate to rabble who could neither govern nor pray properly.

In the cities, pamphlets described her differently. The Lady of the Open Gate. The Vey traitress. The Widow of Greyfen, though Tomas had never been her husband.

She kept none of the pamphlets.

She kept Tomas’s coat.

There was no monument in the courtyard. She refused the proposal when the new council suggested one.

“A statue would only give the rain something else to wear away,” she said.

Instead, she had the gate repaired—not with iron plates and a heavy lock, but with two broad wooden doors that opened inward and outward. Above them, she ordered a simple sentence carved into the lintel:

NO ONE ENTERS HUNGRY. NO ONE LEAVES IN CHAINS.

The work was done by the Dallows’ eldest daughter, who had learned masonry from the men rebuilding East Hollow. When the final letter was cut, she asked whether Tomas’s name should be added.

Elianor touched the rough stone.

“He asked me for a door,” she said. “Not a statue.”

The girl nodded, understanding more than Elianor had explained.

Years passed without making the grief smaller.

It changed its shape instead.

At first Tomas was everywhere: in the woods beyond the ruined lodge, in the crack of a branch, in the smell of wet wool, in the sudden movement of a bird above the ridge. Elianor would turn to tell him something and find only a rain-darkened path.

Later, she could speak his name without losing her breath.

She visited the forester’s lodge each spring. The roof had been repaired and the walls widened. It became a schoolroom, then a meetinghouse for marsh families, then a place where travelers could sleep without paying a lord for permission.

No one was turned away.

Oren survived, though the bullet left him weak in cold weather. He became keeper of the new gate and complained loudly whenever anyone neglected the hinges. Sella recovered enough to work beside Britha in the kitchens. The Dallows reclaimed East Hollow and planted oats where Caelan’s records had once charged them double for every harvest.

Mara remained at Greyfen, older, sharper, and impossible to dismiss. She and Elianor argued over nearly everything except the doors.

By the fifth year, the west wing had been taken down stone by stone. Its beams were used for cottages, bridges, and a new roof over the grain store. The hall became a public house of records, though the records no longer belonged to one family. Copies were kept in three villages, and no single lord could burn a people’s history in one night.

The original ledger was gone.

Elianor sometimes regretted that.

She remembered the pages curling black, the figures vanishing in flame, the terrible relief of destroying the weapon that had ruled Greyfen. Evidence had been lost with the cruelty. Names, debts, signatures, and years of suffering had disappeared.

So the new courts kept better records.

Every payment was read aloud. Every labor agreement was witnessed. Every judgment could be challenged. The people had learned that paper could be a chain, but they had also learned that it could be a key.

On the anniversary of the revolt, Elianor walked to the hill above the manor.

The rain had begun before dawn. It silvered the rebuilt roofs and filled the old foundation trenches. Below her, the open gate stood bright against the dark stone. Children crossed beneath it carrying baskets of bread. A farmer led two oxen through. Someone had left flowers on the lintel, though no one knew who.

Beyond the gate, the road ran toward the marsh, repaired and broad enough for carts.

No sentry stopped the travelers.

No steward demanded their names.

Elianor rested her hand against the wet stone and looked toward the ridge.

For an instant, a goshawk appeared there, circling crookedly in the rain. It rose, dipped, and rose again.

She thought of Tomas beneath the burning gate, asking her to carry the people out. She thought of his hand in hers at dawn, his voice already fading, his final insistence that grief must become something larger than itself.

Not a statue.

A door.

Elianor watched the bird vanish into the brightening clouds.

Then she went down the hill to open the stores.
